translation:
The first volume of the Canon of Medicine,
composed by the Chief Master Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina al-Bukhari.
It contains:
The First Book,
which concerns the Universals (general principles of medicine),
and the Second Book,
on simple (compound) drugs.

translation:
Right page:

In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, and may God's blessings be upon our master Muhammad the Noble.
Praise be to God with praise befitting His abundant grace, and blessings upon Muhammad and his family and servants. I have sought to extract for myself, and for one who has not found a name for himself in medicine, a way to seek healing through reference to universal principles and particular things, so as not to need to gather rare ingredients or go without fulfilling most needs.
To make this accessible, I resolved not to speak of matters in their totality in general terms. First I will describe the natural methods of medicine, then after that the universal principles and properties of simple drugs, then their combinations, then after that the diseases occurring in each organ, beginning first with a description of that organ and its function. The primary organs and their simple drugs first, then the description thereof, which is in the first book — the kidneys and likewise the description of their functions — then when I have finished describing that organ...

Left page:

I begin the most important sections by mentioning how to preserve health, then follow that with a universal statement of its requirements, causes, methods of reasoning about them, and ways to address them. Having dealt with these universal matters, I move to particular diseases, mentioning them also under the universal headings, and then — God willing — detailing them. Then come the universal laws, then the treatments, then I descend to particular matters of simple and compound remedies, those whose composition comes from simple drugs, and the matters of simple drugs. Then when dealing with small quantities and the uses of pigments in their application, when I reach that point, even if the universal details are few, and what are compound medicines — the other kind — when tested, I believe that the learned will understand their composition and how to mix them. I resolved that when I finish this, the book will be a complete work. Also, particular matters not specifically concerned with diseases will be mentioned there as well, along with discussion of related topics also in this book, following the method of the abridged book. When this book is finished, and if God grants me the ability to complete it, I regard it as a book unmatched by any other, and this book is not for those who are weak in the art. How can the rules of medicine be known and memorized if...

On the minimum that nature requires of the body — as for exceeding it, that is a matter not easily regulated. If one is to avoid something, it is better not to set secondary limits for it. As for the present arrangement, this book relies on five books organized as follows: The First Book on the science of medicine. The Second Book on simple drugs. The Third Book on particular diseases affecting the organs of the human body, one organ after another, from top to bottom and what surrounds them. The Fourth Book on particular diseases that arise at certain times and affect specific organs. The Fifth Book on compound drugs, which concerns diseases in general. The First Book contains two arts: The First Art concerns the natural principles of things. The section on the classification of diseases, their causes, and general symptoms. The Third Art on the preservation of health. The Fourth Art on the classification of general treatment according to general and particular diseases. The First Art has six teachings: The First Teaching is on medicine itself, its subject and purpose, and its foundations. The Second Teaching. The Third Teaching on mixture. The Fourth Teaching. The Fifth Teaching on direction. The Sixth Teaching on spirits, faculties, and actions. The First Teaching has two chapters. The Second Chapter defines medicine and classifies its types. The Second Chapter. The Third Teaching has three chapters: The First Chapter on the composition of the Second Teaching within it.

THE FIRST CHAPTER OF THE BOOK OF UNIVERSALS IN MEDICINE

The first thing we ought to know at the outset concerns the states of the human being, in terms of health and its departure, and the descent into illness. One might say that medicine is divided into theory and practice, so that every theoretical element could be called a science. We must say that it is said that among the arts there are those that are theoretical and those that are practical, just as this is said of philosophy — that medicine has a theoretical part and a practical part. The meaning in each division of the terms "theoretical" and "practical" is something other than the general philosophical usage; this applies specifically to medicine. It must be made clear that part of medicine is theoretical in nature, dealing with knowledge and instruction, while another part is practical. This is clarified by those who have examined this subject. We should know that this means something further: no one of the premises of medicine can stand alone as pure knowledge — rather, it functions as a report about how one approaches the first principles, what is called "knowledge" or "theory," while the second is called "practice" in terms of what actually brings the theoretical conviction into reality. Among the matters of conviction it is said that medicine, when its methods are compared, has instruction as its second component, while practical action leads toward causes and measures that are limitless. All of this is organized under the division of medical knowledge, since instruction in medicine begins when it is connected to the manner of application.

Left page:

As is said in medicine, the matters that must be examined concern the conditions that are necessary for the human being to maintain health and prevent its loss, and how this is to be achieved. Certain ideas emerge from this, supported by established principles, having to do with the analysis of compounds and medications, and with the composition from materials that pertain to the natural organs — all of which is encompassed in this knowledge. One must explain in what manner the knowledge of these things is attained. It must also be stated that we are speaking about a single aspect of the states of the human body. In what follows we shall mention that disease and its variations are classified according to the active principle involved. Between these two positions there is no room for an intermediate path, nor for incidental occurrences. We further state that in discussing deficiency one must account for disease in relation to the three states we have established: direct contact, illness itself — which encompasses the functions that have deviated from their proper origins — and the normal balanced state, as well as its opposite. Regarding these realities, one must verify deficiency and the conditions stipulated, without involving ourselves in a dispute among physicians on this point, for this is not something they contest in the same way, nor does it lead anywhere. Its benefit in medicine is to verify these matters for those who adhere to the principles of the art.

THE SECOND CHAPTER ON THE SUBJECT OF MEDICINE

Since medicine examines the states of health and illness from the standpoint of both knowledge and practice in a comprehensive manner, it achieves its full value only when the underlying causes are known — for one cannot truly learn medicine without knowing its causes.

text:
Right page:

الصحة والمرض ولأنا الصحة والمرض قد كونا ظاهرين معه
يكونا تخفيين لأنا لا نالهما بالاستدلال من العوارض فيجب أن
يعرفية الطبيب الأول أن يتعرف الصحة والمرض وقد قدمنا من قبل العلم
الحقيقية أن العلم بالشواهد ما يحصل الهم بالأسباب وبادئ أن كانت
له وان لم نكن من جهة الهم بعوارضه ولو لا زمه الذاتية لكون الأشياء
أربعة أصناف مادية وفاعلية وصورية وقابمه والأسباب المادية
في الأشياء الموضوعة التي تقترب الصحة والمرض الأمر الموضوع لأقرب
وزيق وأما الموضوع للأخلاط فهي الأسباب الفاعلة وأما الأركان فأنه
موضوعان يحسب التركيب وأن كان الاستقالة الاصناف كلا فأنه
يأتي في مركبه واسحالة الثا الوصد في هذا الموضع الشيء
ثلث تلك الأكثرة أما المزاج وأما الهيئة التي المدة وأما الهيئة
فيصب التركيب وأما الأسباب الفاعلة فعلى المعنيين أولها الحفظ لها
بدن الإنسان من الأوهة وما يتصل بها من الطعام والمياه والمشارب وما
يصل بها والاستفراغ والاحتقان والبلدان والمساكن وما يصل بها
والحركات والسكونات لبدنية والنفسانية ومنها النوم واليقظة والاحتياج

Left page:

في الإنسان ولا الاختلاف فيها وفي الأجناس والصناعات والعادات والأشياء الواردة
على البدن الإنسان في ما سعد له أما بمخالفة الطبيعة وإما بالقية الطبيعة وأما
الصورية فالمزاجات والقوى الحاذة بذوعها والمركب والأسباب القابلة فالانفال
وفي معرفة الأفعال معرفة القوى لأحالها ومعرفة الأرواح الحاملة للقوى كاسباب
فهو موضوعاتها صناعة الطبيب من هذا ما يحاول الإنسان بدن أن يكفيح
ويخرج فيما تأمر به تام وهو أن يحفظ الصحة وجزء من مزيل لأمراض يجب
يكون البضالا الأجزاء أنجر مخبل الأسباب الأثرين والأبناء والأسباب ثلاث
ثلاثة بالزوال أول الأمريض بالخيار الهوى ولقد أدبر الهركية والمرض
بالداء والعلاج ولا لذكر كذلك الأطباء يحسب ثلاث صنائع أحدها والعلاج والمرض
والمتوسطين الذين ذكر وهم كيف هم متوسطون من صنفين لا تواسطة
بينهما في الحقيقة وإن ذمصنفصلنا هذه أبيناها بعد نجتمع إن الطب
ينظر الأركان والمزاجات والأخلاط والأصناء والأصناء لا بسيطة والمركبة
والأرواح وقواها الطبيعية والنفسانية والحيوانية والأفعال والحال
من الصحة والمرض وتشتمد وتشبثه والأسباب المآكل والمشارب ولا هوية
المياه والبلدان والمساكن والاستفراغ والاحتقان والأعفان والصناعات والأعمال
translation:
Right page:

Health and disease, since health and disease may be manifest or hidden, and we do not reach them except by inference from their symptoms, it is necessary for the physician first to know how to identify health and disease. We have previously established that true knowledge is that which is acquired concerning causes, and that if things have essential concomitants, things fall into four categories: material, efficient, formal, and receptive. The material causes in things that relate to health and disease are the proximate subject matter. As for the subject of the humors, these are the efficient causes. As for the elements, they serve as the substrate in two respects according to composition. Even if the qualities are of all kinds, they come together in their composition. The discussion of this subject involves three things: the temperament, the constitution as it pertains to the body's condition, and the structure as it pertains to composition. As for the efficient causes, they operate in two senses: first, the preservation of the human body from harm and what is connected to it, such as food, water, and beverages, and what is related to them — evacuation, retention, regions, and dwellings, and what is connected to them — bodily and psychic motions and rest, among them sleep, wakefulness, and retention.

Left page:

In the human being and the differences therein, and in the species, arts, habits, and things that act upon the body — whether by opposing nature or by following nature — as for the formal causes, they are the temperaments, the faculties that arise from them, the composite structure, and the receptive causes which are the actions. In knowing the actions, one knows the faculties in their states, and knowledge of the spirits that carry the faculties is among the foundations. These are the subjects of the art of medicine: what the physician aims at with respect to the human body is to preserve it and to remove disease. It is therefore necessary that the causes be divided into those that precede and those that follow, and the causes are of three kinds. The removal of disease is first by choosing favorable air, then by regulating motion and rest, by treating the disease, and the physicians according to their three categories: those concerned with treatment and disease, and those in between, who are mentioned as intermediaries between two classes, with no true middle ground between them. If we were to enumerate all of this in detail, we would have shown it completely. In sum, medicine examines the elements, temperaments, humors, simple and compound organs, the spirits and their natural, psychic, and vital faculties and actions, states of health and disease, and what causes and maintains them — including foods, beverages, waters, regions, dwellings, evacuations, retentions, putrefactions, crafts, and activities.

text:
الصفحة اليمنى:

وللحركات البدنية والنفسانية والتكوينات والإنسان والإنسان ما يراد
على البدن من الأمور الغريبة والتدبير في المطاعم والمشارب وإبقاء الهواء وتعهد
الحركة والتكون والأدوية والحال المغيرة الجملة لحفظ الصحة وعلاج مرض
فبعض هذه الأمور إنما تجب عليه من جهة ما هو طبيب أن يتصور بما يحقق
تصوراً وعلماً وتصديقاً فاعلاً ثم وضع له مقبول من صالح علم
الطبيعي وبعضها يلزمه أن يمرن عليه في صناعته فإن كان من هذه كالمبادئ
فيلزمه أن يقلد هليها فإن مبادئ العلوم الجزئية مثبتة وتبرهن في العلوم
العامة ومنها كذلك تشبق مبادئ العلوم كلها إلى الفلسفة الأولى التي
طالع إلينا بعد الطبيعة وإذا أسرع بعض المتطببين فأخطأ في إثبات
وتفرج من الناتج لذه العلم الطبيعي ما هو موضوع فإنه مغلط من جهة ثم
يورد في صناعة الطب ما ليس من صناعة الطب ويغلط من حيث تبيين شيئاً
ولا يكون تدبيبه البتة فالذي يجب أن يتصور الطبيب بالماهية ويتولد
منه ما كان يسير من الجملة هو منه الأركان البتة ويتفنذ
وكيفو والمزاجات وإهالها وكهو وابن في كل تقتذ
حال وابن أسبابها وكو في والأن الأعضاء ومن أفم يجب

الصفحة اليسرى:

وبمعالجة فما بالحس والتجريب والذين يجيبون يتصون ويبرهنون عليه الأمراض ولسباب
التجربة وعلاماتها وأنه كيف نازل المرض وحفظ الصحة فإنه لازمه
البرهان على ما كان من هذه المنهج الوجود بتفصيله وتعقيبه وتوقيته وبالثبور
إذا الحاول في إقامة البرهان على كل ما الفسلاول فإنه يحاول ذلك من جهة
طبيب ولكنه من جهة فيلسوف فيكون كلامه من الطبيعي علم الفقه إن
اذا الحاول أن يبرهن على صحة الأحتياج تابعة من المنهج فإنه من جهة المنهج
وكون ما هو من جهة حكم الطبيب ولكن من جهة ما هو طبيب ومن
ليبرهن كه على ذلك والواقع الدور
التعليم الثاني الأركان
وغرض العلم أحد الأركان في أجسام سطة أولية بدن الإنسان
وعيره التي لايمكن أن تنقسم اجسام مختلفة الصور ولا يمتزج بها وإليها
الأنواع المختلفة منها كالكائنات الطبيعية من الطبيبي لها أربعة أصناف
منها خفيفان وثقيلان وأنثيان فأشد خفيفان فالنار والهواء والثقيلان الأرض
والماء ولا أرض بل جرم بسيط موضعه الطبيعي الكل وسط الكائنات
وتحرك إليه الطبيع إذا كان مباينا وذلك بفعله المطلق وهو يبارد بما بل
في طبيعته إذا طلع ما يوجبه ولو بعير من سبب من خارج طبعه وذ
translation:
Right page:

Concerning bodily and psychological movements, constitutions, and what is required of the body in terms of external matters, management of food and drink, preservation of air, care of movement and constitution, medicines, and the general conditions for preserving health and treating disease. Some of these matters require the physician to conceptualize and know them truly and with active conviction, based on what is accepted from the sound principles of natural science. Some require him to practice them in his craft. If they are among the foundational principles, he must follow them, for the principles of particular sciences are established and demonstrated in the general sciences, and from these all the principles of the sciences ascend to First Philosophy, which we encounter after natural science. When some practitioners rush and err in establishing these foundations, they go wrong in the subject of natural science, introducing into medical practice what does not belong to it, making errors in explanation. The physician must therefore form a conceptual understanding of the essence of things, and from this will derive the elements, temperaments, their qualities, and every condition, causes, organs and their benefits.

Left page:

As for treatment by sense and experience: those who respond to these describe and demonstrate diseases, their causes and symptoms, how illness progresses, and how health is preserved. All that is demonstrated through this method is worked out in detail, sequentially, and with proper timing. But if one attempts to establish proofs for everything, he does so as a philosopher rather than a physician, and his discourse comes from natural philosophy rather than from medicine. If he attempts to demonstrate the validity of inference through method, he does so from a methodological standpoint, which belongs to the physician as physician.

The Second Lesson: The Elements
The subject of this science is one of the elements found in simple, primary bodies of the human body and others, which cannot be divided into bodies of different forms and cannot be mixed. The different types among natural bodies are of four kinds: two light and two heavy. The two light ones are fire and air; the two heavy ones are earth and water. The earth is a simple body whose natural place is the center of all existing things. Nature moves toward it when separated from it by its own absolute action. It is cold and moist by nature when what requires this emerges, even without an external cause outside its nature.

text:
[Right page:]
محسوس ويبرو وجوده في الكائنات وجود منبط للاسمات والمثبتات وحفظ
الاشكال والهيئات وأما الماء فهو جرم بسيط موضعه الطبيعي كرة
شاملة للارض مشمولا للهواء إذا كان على وضعه الطبيعي وهو يقبله
الامنا في وهو يارد رطباً يطبعه البلع إذا خلط وما يوجبه وطبيعاً ضده سبب
من خارج لظهر عنه برد محسوس وسال من رطوبة وكوّن في جملته حيث يجب يفيد
سبيل الاول يتخذ ويقبل المشكل كما ثم لا يحفظه ووجوده في الكائنات
لتسلسل الهيئات لمادية اجزاءها من التشكيل والحفيظة والتقديل فان الطب
وان كان سهل المثلة المهيئات الشكلية فهوسما لقبولها اليابس وان
كان زعر المقبول للمهيئات الشكلية فهوعسر الترك لها وهو ما تحن اليابس الرطب
إسناداً اليابس من ليابسه لقبولا للتشكيل شهد له الطب اليابس
حفظ الأحداث فيه من المقوم والتقديل قريبا لقي الطب اليابس من شتم ثم
واسماء الرطب اليابس بزند وأما الهواء فهو جرم بسيط موضعه
الطبيعي فوق الماء وتحت خفية الامناط وطبعه ما وبارد رطب
ووجوده في الكائنات المتحلل ويلطف ويخف وينفل وأما
النار فهو جرم بسيط موضعه الطبيعي فوق الامن ما العنصر كلها

[Left page:]
ومكانها الطبيعي ما سطح المتقعر من المثلث الذي ينبئ عنده اكون والفسادليّا
وذلك بثبتها المطلقة وطبعها الحار إيرو وجودها في الكائنات لنضج وتنضج
بالامتناع ويجري بها لانفس الجوما لتي ولتكون محومنه به الفضر الماريق
فرعية من الفضرية التي المزاجية والطبائل الاذون ثنية في الكائنا وسكونها وتنبيه
عون تكون الخارج لا الاعضاء وفي تحريك بها وفي جملة الأول
الاول هو الفصل من وان لا اركان التعليم الثالث الثانية فصولب
الفصل الاولية المنهاج المنهاج كيف تشدد من تفاعل اجزاء متضادة
موجودة في ضمايرمنصفة الاجزاء أما لكركز ولصلمتها الاجزاء الفاعلات
منوا لنفسها في مضمونها أن تجملها كيف منتشابه في جميعها لا مزاج ولا قوة
الاولية في الاركان الاربعة المذكورة الحرارة والبرودة والرطوبة واليبوسة فيئن
المزاجيات من الاجسام والكائنة الماركون وذلك لما تجابسا وحينا
المثمة العملية بالنظر المطلق غير مضاف وعلى وجهه وإسهاب الوجهان
التميز ان يكون المزاج معلما لكل الامناد ويكون الكائنات متضادة في الشمص
مساوية متقاومة ويكون المزاج متوسطة بينها وأن ان المزاج الثاني الا
كونا المزاج بين كيفيات متضادة ومطلقاً وسطاً ويكون مايل الى احد الطرفين
translation:
[Right page:]
It is perceptible, and its existence in created things is as a substrate for forms and stable qualities, and for the preservation of shapes and configurations. As for Water, it is a simple body whose natural place is a sphere encompassing the earth, itself encompassed by air, when it is in its natural position. It receives and is cold and moist in its nature; when mixed, it accepts form. Whatever opposes it causes, by external means, a perceptible coldness to appear from it, and it flows with moisture, and forms in its totality where required. It serves as the first recipient and accepts form, but does not preserve it. Its existence in created things enables the continuation of configurations, for the material parts of forms, through shaping, preservation, and modification. If something is easily disposed to receive forms, it is apt to receive the dry; and if it is difficult for forms to be received, it is reluctant to release them — this is what draws the dry-moist together. The dry lends itself to shaping; medicine attests to this. The dry preserves what has been formed and is close to the modification of moisture. As for Air, it is a simple body whose natural place is above water and below the concavity of the fiery sphere; its nature is warm and moist. Its existence in created things causes dissolution, refinement, lightness, and movement. As for Fire, it is a simple body whose natural place is above all other elements.

[Left page:]
Its natural place is the concave surface of the innermost sphere, adjacent to the region of generation and corruption. This is established by its absolute quality and its hot temperament. Its existence in created things brings about ripening and maturation. Through it, the souls of living things are sustained, and through it, the active faculty is enabled to work upon matter. From this arise the temperamental and natural faculties of created beings, their stability, and their activation. Through it, the limbs are moved and their functions sustained. The first section concerns the elements.

The First Section: The Method — How the interaction of mutually opposing parts occurs. These opposing parts exist within a unified body, concentrated and acting upon one another. They spread through the whole of the body so that it becomes uniform in all its parts, with neither a distinct temperament nor a primary quality prevailing. The four primary qualities present in the four aforementioned elements — heat, cold, moisture, and dryness — interact in bodies and created things when they come into contact with one another. The practical consideration, taken absolutely without qualification and in its proper sense, is that the temperament becomes a universal measure for all the opposing qualities, so that the opposing qualities in the compound become equal and balanced, and the temperament stands as a mean between them. The second type of temperament exists between mutually opposing qualities in an absolute and intermediate sense, yet inclines toward one of the two extremes.

text:
الصفحة اليمنى:

أما في أحد المتضادين فهما البرودة والحرارة والرطوبة واليبوسة وأما قليلهما
لكن المعتبر في صناعة الطب بالاعتدال والخروج عن الاعتدال وليس هذا ولا ذلك الـسبيل
بل يجب أن يعلم الطبيب أن الطبيعي المعتدل كيف هذا المعنى وأن يجوز أن يوجد بدله
عن أن يكون مزاج إنسان أو عضو إنسان وإن بعيد أن المتعادل المتة تتملى
الاعتدال بمن هو مشتق لأمن التعادل الذي هو التوازن بتسوية
بل من المدلول المقسمة وهوان يكون قد توفر فيه المهزج بما كأن كان
بتمامه وعضوان من العناصر بكياتها وكيفياتها أن اللسط الذي ينبغي لذيقة
مزاج الإنسان على اعتدل قسمة وفيتة بلغ كده قد يمر أن تكون من ذيه
قسمة أن ثنا نشرف يجعل الاثنان قريباً جداً من المعتدل الحقيقي الأولى
وهذا الاعتدال المقترب يجب بأن الناس أيضاً الذي هو اعتدال القياس إلى
غير ما ليرلهذا اعتداله وليس له وليقبل الإنسان من الاعتدا لـ
المذكورة في الوجه الأول لقرض له ثمانية أوجه من الاعتبا رات
فأنثه أما أن يكون مقيساً للنوع مقيساً لما هو خارج
وأما أن يكون مقيساً للنوع مقيساً لما يختلف قاهو في
وأما أن يكون مقيساً من صنف مقيساً الى ما يختلف ما هو خارج عنه

الصفحة اليسرى:

وفي نوعه وأما أن يكون بحسب صنفه منا لنوع مقيساً الى ما يختلف قاهو فيه
وأما أن يكون بحسب المحضر من الصنف مقيساً الى ما يختلف خارج عنه
وفي صنفه ونوعه وأما أن يكون بحسب المحضر مقيساً الى ما يختلف من أحوال
نفسه وأما أن يكون بحسب المضموم مقيساً الى ما يختلف خارج عنه ويؤدب منه
وأما أن يكون بحسب المضموم مقيساً الى أحواله التي فيه فالقسم الأول
هو المعتدل الحقيقي المطلق الذي هو اعتدال القياس سار إذ كان أياتهم وليترخص
فيه وليسلك أيضاً القياس بلا افراط والقرب منهما أن يكون إنسان وإنسان
بطلى المزاج عن مزاج إنسان وأما الثالث والوسط بين المزاج
المرض وبه يتميز يخص صفة غاية الاعتدال وهو الكمال في الاعتدال
للسن الذي يبلغ فيه السن إلى غاية القوة وهذا أيضا ما يقرب لا
الحقيقي وهذا كذلك لا يكون لكن تثبت إذ كانت فيه أعضاؤه الحارة كالقلب والبارة
كالدماغ والطبيعة كالكبد والبانية كما كالعظام فإذا توازنت وتعادلت
قريب من المعتدل الحقيقي لأن المعتدل كل عضو فيه كاعضو
واحده وهو الجلال على أنه لا بد ولما بالقياس إلى الأرواح والى الإضافة
الرتبه ثم بعد ذلك نكون مقارناً لـأن الاعتدال الحقيقي بل خارج عنه

الحاشية:
وهذا ايضاً لأن يكون الحقيقي الميد المكون بنيل أبعاله المضلوحى تبعاً فإنه جائز وجوده
translation:
Right page:

As for one of the two opposites, they are coldness and heat, and moisture and dryness, and as for their lesser forms — but what is truly considered in the art of medicine is the state of equilibrium and deviation from equilibrium. Neither this nor that is the way to proceed. Rather, the physician must know what constitutes the natural temperament and equilibrium, and understand that it is possible to find instead of it the temperament of a human being or the temperament of an organ, even if it is far from the balanced and equalized state. The equilibrium is derived from those who speak of balance, meaning proportionality and equalization. Rather, from the indicated divisions, it means that the temperament has been fully realized with the proper amounts and qualities of the elements in their quantities and qualities, as is required for the precise temperament of the human being. In terms of proportion and degree, it may happen that from a given portion, the two are very close to the true equilibrium — the primary one. This approximate equilibrium, which is necessary, is what people also call the relative standard of measurement, which is different from that absolute equilibrium. For this reason, it is not possible for a person to attain the equilibrium mentioned in the first aspect, so there are eight aspects of consideration for it: First, it may be measured for the species as measured against what is external to it; or it may be measured for the species as measured against what differs within it; or it may be measured from one type as measured against what is external to it that differs.

Left page:

And within its species. Or it may be measured according to its type within the species as compared to what differs within it. Or it may be measured according to the particular member of the type as compared to what differs and is external to it and its type and species. Or it may be measured according to the particular member as compared to what differs from its own states. Or it may be measured according to what is compounded with it as compared to what differs from what is external to it and is derived from it. Or it may be measured according to what is compounded as compared to its own states within it. The first division is the absolute true equilibrium, which is the standard of measurement in general — since it pertains to all — and one should not be too lenient about it, and one should also follow the standard without excess. Closest to it are those two: a human being whose temperament is modeled on the temperament of a human, and the third is the mean between temperaments. Through this, the particular characteristic of the utmost equilibrium is distinguished, which is the perfection of balance — the age at which one reaches the fullness of strength. This too is close to, but not exactly, the true equilibrium, and this likewise does not truly exist. However, it is established in one in whom the hot organs such as the heart, and the cold ones such as the brain, and the natural ones such as the liver, and the structural ones such as the bones are all in balance and proportion. When they are balanced and equalized, one is close to the true equilibrium, since the equilibrium of each organ is like that of every other organ. This is the perfection, subject to the condition that there must also be a relation to the vital spirits and to the other relationships of rank. After that, it would be approximating the true equilibrium, though still outside it.

Marginal note:
This also applies because the true equilibrium constituted by the full actualization of its proper functions in succession is possible in its existence.

translation:
Right page:

Concerning heat and moisture: the source of life is the heart and the vital spirit, and when these incline toward excess, the body cannot sustain life through heat and moisture alone, for it is heat that maintains the spirit and nourishes it. The principal organs are three, as previously mentioned, and the coldest among them is the brain; and it does not suit the heart if the heat of the heart is not tempered, for the heart tends toward dryness; and the heart's dryness cannot be compensated by the moisture of the brain and liver, nor can the brain compensate the liver in this way either, nor does the heart's temperament suit one that is dry. The brain is the fourth among them. As for the Third Section:

This is a temperament derived from the first, which is the ideal, but it possesses a relative equilibrium suited to a particular people according to their climate and region. These are the people whose temperament inclines toward deviation from the ideal, each measured by reference to their own nature. As for comparison by country: if one considers the temperament of a Macedonian measured against India, and likewise the condition of an independent country against the temperament of an Indian, then each one is well-suited and adequate — each having a temperament fitting and appropriate to its own climate, though it has extremes of excess and deficiency. As for the Fourth Section: it is intermediate between the two extremes.

Left page:

It is the standard of the region's climate, and it is the most balanced of that category. As for the Fifth Section: it is a temperament derived from the first and third sections combined, and it is the temperament that ought to exist in a living, healthy individual. It also has two extremes, of excess and deficiency, and it is possible to determine the temperament of each person individually, though it is not possible for it to share in the other extreme. As for the Sixth Section: it is intermediate between these two limits, and it is also the most balanced and excellent temperament that ought to exist.

As for the Seventh Section: it is the temperament that ought to characterize each individual organ. It is well known that proper balance differs by organ — in bone, dryness should predominate; in the brain, moisture should predominate; in the heart, heat should predominate; and in the muscles, coldness should predominate. This temperament also has extremes of excess and deficiency, though less extreme than those mentioned in the introduction.

As for the Eighth Section: it is the mean between these two limits, and it is the temperament that ought ideally to be attained for all ages and conditions. When these statements are examined, the one closest to the truth is that of the human being. When all three are considered together, what is lost among them is best understood when found in the balanced genus at the equinox, and God knows best.

translation:
Right Page:

Among the earthly causes are the mountains and seas, and it must be that they are the closest types to true temperament. Although what occurs here is a deviation from temperament, the cause is the proximity of the sun. The sun's direct rays reaching the area contribute to preserving the air from corruption. Here, most importantly, when the seasons arrive, the conditions of the dominant humors are similar, and the air does not oppose them in a contradictory way but rather matches their bodily constitution. These types are inhabitants of no single clime, for they exist without the intermediary of the sun above their heads, like inhabitants of the second and third climes. Unlike those upon whom the sun shines directly, like inhabitants of the hottest fifth clime. As for what is above them, and as for absorption, it is well established that the organs most distant from true temperament are not truly balanced but incline toward what God has determined. The organs closest to that temperament are the skin, which barely reacts to water mixed equally half boiling and half cold, yet interacts well.

Left Page:

Within it, the blood thickens, and the deposit settles, so it does not act uniformly throughout the mixture. When it is in a body and its most tractable parts are equally balanced, it does not act because nothing analogous occurs. The reason why places do not react is that when something is contrary to it, it does not act upon it in the same way. For the element of opposition among natures, each acts upon the other, and most of this occurs through the sharing of qualities — when there is a sharing of quality, there is similarity. The skin most resembles the next skin in temperament, then the skin of the arm, then what is on the fingers, then the palms, then the extremities of the fingers. This is how the governing faculty measures what passes to it, for the judge must be equally inclined toward both extremes in order to deviate from them. As we have established, we determined that blood, if it were truly balanced, we could not call it possible, and it does not remain in that true equilibrium. Therefore, true balance is not achievable in reality, and what remains is relative balance. The place from the human substance being determined is more numerous.

translation:
Right Page:

Note that when the innate heat acts upon the human body, and however its quality may be, that quality is not a specific characteristic of the human constitution in either extreme of departure from balance and moderation, nor does it produce effects that compensate toward moderation. Rather, it is judged not by the standard of what it does in the human body. Likewise, when we say something is hot or cold, we do not mean that it is so in all of its remaining heat or coldness, nor that the thing is hotter or colder in its substance than the human body. Nor is the standard that of something equivalent to the human constitution's temperament. Rather, we find in the human body heat or coldness beyond what is mild for them, and this can make something cold in relation to the medical standard of the human body, yet hot in relation to iron; and hot in relation to the human body, yet cold in relation to iron. Indeed, one thing may be hot in relation to one thing and cold in relation to another. Physicians have long debated this: whether the temperament is such as to not conflict, and we have explained the distinction between the balanced and the unbalanced. We now say: the unbalanced, whether judged by species, type, or harm — what causes participation in measuring the balanced — those measures testify to this approach.

Left Page:

What deviates from balance is either simple or compound, combined in two opposing qualities. The simple deviation in active qualities is such that it may become each individually — either drier than it should be, or colder than it should be, or moister, or hotter — without the passive quality necessarily accompanying it. That is because it may be as dry as it should be yet cold, and not as moist as it should be yet not hot or cold. And if one considers that the four qualities require that the constitution of a place be as moist as needed, not dry, and as the four qualities require in this regard — then the compound deviations are those that arise from opposition between combined active qualities: either hotter and moister together than they should be, or colder and drier together, or colder and moister together, or hotter and drier together. It is impossible for something to be simultaneously hotter and colder, or simultaneously moister and drier. Each deviation either occurs without matter — meaning that the temperament of the body arises in the body —

Right page:

How temperaments are constituted without the body having previously been conditioned by them: mixtures may combine in a body's composition — for example, the body's warmth may be combined with the cold of snow and ice, without there being any substance involved — and the body may not adapt itself to that temperament. Three qualities generally intermix in it, such as the ripening of the non-human body through adjustment and modification, as discussed in Books Three and Four, where no single thing corresponds to another alone.

When a temperament involves a material component, the organ may sometimes have the capacity to absorb that material, or it may sometimes pass through quickly, or the material may become trapped in its channels and pathways. Based on what was needed and how it was used, something nutritive and refined results. This is the discussion of the classification of humors and their qualities.

The Fourth Chapter: On the manner by which the constitution and condition in every case — all of which flow from the temperament, either by what agrees with it or what conflicts — can be understood. As for verifying this, it is the philosopher's task, not the physician's. As for man, if he has a balanced temperament, it is possible for this to apply to each organ according to its appropriate quality, with some organs being warmer, some colder, some drier, and some more moist. As for what is within our bodies — the spirit and the heart, which is the source of it all...

Left page:

When what remained of it was something that had settled in the liver and then descended into the body, it settled there as the liver's own settled substance and the organ's remainder. This residue was repelled and returned, and through digestion it absorbed what was drawn up from the hidden inner regions, from the external surface, and from what rises — as God has ordained it. The necessity of this process and its coming together in the daytime was facilitated by an additional measure distributed among the recipients.

Through the passage of these, the inherited material was dissolved and the organs, bones, channels, and vessels all conducted it throughout the body. The governing powers — the containing, the retaining, the expelling — carry out the functions of the body. By the natures of the spirit working within it, a separation occurs that is not truly a separation, which loosens what was condensed and dissolves what was bound. The temperament flows like a philosopher's inquiry into what was separated: something akin to it in temperament, similar to it in constitution, acted upon by the senses in a non-bonded manner.

Thus, what is resolved is loosened by its subtlety and thinness, accepting what the nature of the stars and heavenly bodies determines. When the dwelling is aligned with the dwelling, as the order of dominion over the dwelling operates in truth, with certainty and affirmation...

كالرقيق والمسكان والصلب والملك [illegible] وهو أركب كلا المعلق كل المكرم بالأليم

translation:
Right page:

The Eighth Chapter: On the most typical cases of black bile in bodies. The fifth group concerns the natural pathway of black bile as a natural blood constituent — not in the manner of a command, but in the manner of dual causation. For the harmful and erring elements bear no proportion to the natural faculty in matters relating to God. The natural black bile and the quality of wine are similar in their temperament. Other factors increase black bile. The chapter on the nature of black bile and the surplus humor demonstrates what we have established. The cause is not merely the consumption of thin foods — for four reasons in my view — since the complete rational faculty has no limit in it. Its duration extends over two periods without end, and the blood within the body has no final cause. At two endpoints of the mentioned periods, if the liver's quality is controlled, then the natural flow would proceed, and the surplus from the compound would be driven away. This preservation depends on the self and its proper function. If it was natural, then the need would be for the faculty to assume its place in the written record. There is no restriction if God's direction guides its management. If the natural black bile is of poor quality, its intensity and heat intensify.

Left page:

The complete preservation is fulfilled when the wave of excess is contained, as written in the book of natural temperament. Natural temperament, like the natural faculty, gathers from certain surplus individuals. The sign indicates three types of cold natural humors. This type teaches what we have mentioned. The natural faculty is slow in its function, and guidance comes from nourishment and what feeds the harmful organs. The humors in a person, if natural, operate when the body is full. They begin from the sluggish matters, and what the sluggish matters have caused — as God said: "They prevailed over the earth" — through the bodily organs. The pure elements that consume thin foods overcome the diet and the thick. The natural and slow matters mix with the humors and seek to correct the disturbed humors. For these thick humors — which pass through the body and draw the best from the composition — when the rational faculty is more solid than the pen's flow, it prevents the person from what harms him, and the surplus corrects itself. If the temperament is natural in a solid mixture without external deviation, the system of the body in its parts — such as the thin, dense, and solid — are all governed by proper measure. The urine also carries these elements, as does the watery black bile and what has passed through the humors.

translation:
Right page:

These are among the drinks that are stimulating and beneficial, and among its properties for us and its passages: As for the mixture of the false and the drink, it suffices for what we need, and what is distant from our people remains for them. It is appropriate not to use an intermediary unless the virgin faculty is complete and the liver is sound, and whatever coagulates is transformed. The humors are drawn from the blood and from the people, and the humors flow without obstruction. One should resemble what accompanies it, so that the human being among them is aided from two abodes. It is necessary for each organ to preserve itself, and for each to accompany the other in regulation. The preservation of transmission is among the most important matters to consider. Things are arranged according to their times, and the humors are diminished in quantity. This is because the faculty does not sustain for long, and it is as though it smooths out. When the corrupt and the spoiled material is present, the rivers carry it along. The benefit is accepted from the seeker and the one who receives it. The processed and the good foods that are given reach their aim. The digestion proceeds in its stages, and the nourishment passes through the body from first to last.

Left page:

Then, upon reflection on the matter, one must preserve sight completely and take account of what is nourishing and what is sought. The doctor must gather from among the flat substances and the various foods and their combinations. He should examine what is appropriate and beneficial for each organ, as it provides nourishment to the seeker of health. Animals require the most beneficial foods from the liver and what the body demands, so the dog's nature receives training. Whatever is prescribed from the eight kinds of foods and the various categories must be measured and regulated in proportion. These substances enter the liver and are digested, and what is produced from them passes into the vessels. The digestion of the kidney with these substances, if the conditions are met, will proceed appropriately. In every case that is sought, the digestion is complete and proportionate, and the benefit accrues to the body, returning ultimately to what is most beneficial.

translation:
Right page:

On the mutual relationship between the two physicians [the liver and the heart], and the refined and subtle qualities [of their functions], and what is manifest from them. The phlegmatic humor and its long-standing nature, resembling in this regard the soft and moist [organs], and so it becomes a chronic condition of what nourishes and conveys the vital faculties to the organs, which is the established and fixed nourishment. And it is noted that when separated from the liver, it is separated from what is called the settling faculty. The settling organ does not need [this faculty] for a reason — that it removes from it what is recognized. Thus God removes from the kidneys and collects from them what is formed in the liver, and filters it such that the kidneys purify the tears and the moist [substances] from all the nutriment, and conveys the remainder to the bile. And so it flows to the spleen in the channels of the blood circulating in the ruling faculty that governs the liver. And thus, in the veins resembling them, it equalizes the fine veins and the flowing humor. Then into the inner recesses, then into the passing fine threads, then into what is spread throughout the limbs — after the governance of the faculty and what the faculty conveys, that which is devoted to the liver, specifically that which resembles it. The subtle nourishment, the gentle overall nutrition, and its resemblance to the digestive faculty.

Left page:

They are channeled toward the [natural] links, and their causes are the measured proportions sent down in the equivalent of the two remembrances — for the cause of the nutriment derives from the compound nature of the fluid, subtle matter of the bile that comes from the liver — the digestive [faculty] forms and refines, and separates the two remembrances, and so its cause is established. The nutriment flows toward it in days, and when separated from it, the [vital] faculty and what comes of it, the Haroun and the returning [humor], and the liver is settled such that it governs and rectifies the mixtures, and the liver then rules all of the humors. Then in the cavity, then in the vessel of the returning [humor], and what God has made of the mixture and the flowing, and after God willed it, only the black [bile] remains, and so the illness remains. If the physician sees the separated [substance] to be among those not reaching the arteries, it is also of those which prevent them. And for every sound treatment, and what is attributed to it, and the child that is born from it — and so the matter is settled. It often happens that what is used as a remedy by the physician is of a noble and fine quality.

translation:
Right page:

The third matter: one does not attain the preservation of health and the maintenance of the bodily fluids without four things, the first of which is the return of the body to its natural state as is well known. From this first of all comes old age, the subtle [humor] which flows through the known [channels], such that the natural temperament through its heat and moisture does not allow the matter to flow in its accustomed channels as it covers the limbs. Each limb is thus filled with the surplus of the first [humor], which is in the earliest stage like the excess of the humor in the liver, like the two luminaries in their [respective] flows. The blood deteriorates together with the phlegm, and the channels are pained by what has gathered in them, such as the salty and brackish [matters]. The mixed [humor] is like the nutritive [material] and the matter becomes weak. If the condition is mild and the person is able to tolerate it when he eats and exercises moderately, then the humors are easily purged and the predominant humor is most easily expelled. Thus the spirit flows freely, restoring and nourishing [the body], and we know from this that the humors are caused by the conditions of the body. فإن الذكر كالبذر للجنس من أجل لأنفصة منه يكون الجنس عز الله فإن كان عبد الله المعدة فيها فيما فيعد للذكر فيه في الذكر إما أن تمنعها فإن منعها فإن البلغ كلكلك هذا المعتاد التوية أعني ألوع المفعلة فيه أما إذا كان على كل يعلم من الأنفة من الجبر حتى جاء من الجلفة فإنه منهم إذا لكل فإنه البين جبر عمر للجبين فيما إذا البيا فإذا للإبل كشف إولالله يس فإنه يرفق في كل بإلمد بعت أن عامة فعامة للإبل للمند فمع ذلك ولاتمشة أن يقول إن العامل في ذكر ذكر أوفى والمفعمد به في المنبع وفى ما يحبس البوك في مصنافيه في البلوة الأصلة فإلى الذكر أكان يفضل عن الملة إلا أن يوصيه منها بأصل اللي الجامعة من الف والأصال إلى الكابيه منه يكون على طابنيا لا يصر هذا الأذك وكل يملي لا ريش في شن ولا الأكثا يعلم في بين الأصل ما يكون لحمًا ما يحتاجه فضلاً للإصلح أجود إلى ربع فيكل في الوقت في القاسم هذه الطبيعه فضلاً للطبيين فإنه أجود أن يكون كيد يمسح ذكر الله فيولد أعند ما كان يولغن إذك الله والله بولغد من الله وتعيمك التخويل البنا يأتي أقسم من طاسته ودسمه وبعتك الله ومالك السله الحرو يكا لكه وكان من الأعضا أنطلق

Left page:

للمبين فإنه فإنه إذا انفسكل بيجز بإلأصل الحصمتقي لأبمنه فيه يبلغ صح ب كلإ ول وفصل الملتوي منه يكون المنتظم وتسبب وارتدة في الكبيرة في الأرمال وفصل الملتوي منه يكون المنظم وسبب وارتدة وارز دة في ذلك من التلبين إما إذا أنفس بجرأ من ذلك كالعلم به أشعب وما كان مخلوقًا من الله فيا ثبيثت سلا وله بشيل اليه كالجم بولدا وعرم وفيه فقع الموفيه فأدار الملى فيها وما ملكت السوا فإذا أفا أن الذين إن ارعي ملأرت في فين إذن المنين يكون بإلأن يكون اتس ما ألسه والله أخواته لايسث من أوفى وتقول بوقى بإلأصل فإن كان تلبيه من المأمة وتكون ثاني من ذلك والحركة ويكون ثانيا من بلا الحك وكما بجمعا عصبة وملكه ويرد وتوده إلى الملك كل في عصبيه وتقوليكس أن جميع الأجسا الملنوه فيه في المناسب غنافا للسدد كالجلب الأوردة في الشرانات ما لا يفيع بين لا ينتكل أن يتما إذا أما في الجوف من الأعضا والعروف منها هتشيها من الأصمان المسيطا للمبط ابنا فإنا كان فيه جميع الآلاة الملبيه كالجب في الملتسل مأ قال ويكون الله وكلأ لو وأما ما تكلك الكبد والكئر من الموركات والآما إلى الكبد وتكبه قيسب لسبل المنبل وأما الطبيعيه فيه يكثيه كيسه الرئو والملبكه فويكه الأذرد قلبه يخص

هامش:
النثير في الشارح الجامع ع وارد قال وربما كان ذلك جامعاً وقال ربما كان طرق وما ورد مثل تلك الحالات لا بأس بالبيت
translation:
Right page:

The male is like a seed for the species, because from the seminal fluid the species originates by the grace of God. If the stomach is present in what is prepared for the male, then it may block it. If it blocks it, the phlegm accumulates as is customary — meaning the various types of active processes. When every part is known through the fine membrane of the bone until it reaches those among them, then all of it works together for the overall benefit. It is recognized in every part by the extension of veins, and the general function of the organ is fulfilled. Along with that, one should consider that the active element in the aforementioned part works most effectively in the generative function. Whatever controls the flow in its vessels — toward the original fluid — is better separated from the general matter unless directed toward the root of the joint assembly. The fundamental principle within it produces from its substance what constitutes flesh and what is required. The best approach is to consider this within the proper time and proportion of this nature. The physicians hold that the best function is that which produces from the divine measure — generating from what was present. God provides and grants the essential nourishment and formative substance, and the organ is released from what was restricted.

Left page:

For the generative faculty: when it is resolved back to the original pure principle for its sustenance, it reaches correctness. The twisted portion of it becomes organized, causing reversion and increase in the large vessels. Among the transformed matter, whenever it diminishes some of that, knowledge of it increases. Whatever was created from divine origin establishes itself and becomes attached to it like a body that is born. It accumulates in the cavity, controlling the fluid, and dominates what it controls. If the generative elements were to draw moisture from within, they would become established through the original principle, and it would be said that this arrangement comes from the warmth of the faculty, producing two results: movement and a secondary effect. Together they form a unified nerve-like bundle that gives and sends back to the body. Each nerve-like component supports all the physical members joined in their proper proportion, filling the vessels like a channel for the veins and arteries. Whatever does not flow between them cannot be extracted to completion. In the internal cavity, the organs and vessels among them are covered by membranes that surround the deep musculature. Within all this are the necessary instruments of the body like the liver in its context. God forms what is proper. The liver and the other viscera, along with the organs attached to the liver, organize themselves and provide the pathway for the natural faculty, which moves like a mechanism through the lungs and heart and sends it to the liver.

Marginal note:
The commentator notes in the comprehensive explanation: it has been reported, and it was said that this may be combined, and it was said that approaches like these cases are acceptable in practice.

translation:
Right page:

The physician's reference concerns distress and pain, the demanding and the gentle refinement of the pleasant. When the connecting vessels are arranged, whatever organs have subtle properties among them — the best examples being those deposited within, and whatever the tongue describes of its array in part — when the two natures of the heart's temperament exceed their bounds, mixing with the humors and the waves from within, the innermost matter: for every comprehensive law, the inner draws and conducts to the surface and to the depths, that which is known. The horizons, their names and needs, because the most numerous of the pathways are sound in attraction and refinement. They have established foundations, so that surrounding it they treat from all sides, so that it becomes tranquil in what is sought. The solid body, when it manifests the lines of its account, is the cause of obstruction. In the judgment of both, every observer of the rising one found in the whole, making the overall picture swift in its finest form. The foundation of this is in the letters from relief, the subtle letters, those of the Quran. The calligrapher takes from it, and what is elevated is the highest, and to God belongs all praise.

Left page:

In every great line, when all things are as described, and one must know that the noble humor and its elevation and its cognizance, or what God has added except mixing — and just as the deposited follows, when we intend that every natural temperament of the body acts upon the nerves — and these two actions, one of which is the solidifying kind, are from the temperament of the discourse, in the most correct path of governance. The order is thus established by God's will. If this becomes thus, the benefit is clear and the singular is attained. The natural essences, their names and needs, and the nerves, the subtle and the fine in their form. It is not possible for the trusted to reach the distressed one, except by God's will. The balance of the constitution in what is counted is only achieved through the will of God among them. The temperament, from the fire, and the constitution, and the fire of God, thereafter — one reaches a point of intersection. Every traveler of the paths inclines to it, drawn to the interior and the hidden, fearing what lies beneath it, reaching the connection. The region of the compound is established by God: "except God, and it is only through God." And if the temperament in their view is by God's grace, and if one is not patient, then the interior except as submitted is counted. The strength of the humors, as measured, is a suppressor, so say: "To God belongs all dominion and praise." And every part, facilitated through it and through God, is an ever-present support.

translation:
[Right page - main text:]

On the benefits and properties relating to the lower members: whatever was from the limbs, this is what is meant by the temperament. The heart's limbs have their benefit not in their constitution but in their well-being, and the limbs that are compound — their nature is for all, within the two physicians of the brain. What is composed of the skin leads to the chapter on veins.

CHAPTER ONE ON THE JOINTS
The First Section of the Fifth Part: On the Dislocation of the Joints and Their Articulations

On what can be measured from the shoulder: it cannot be compared to the base of the spine. The benefit of measuring the shoulder is such that one can judge the condition of the injury therein. What separates the shoulder from the joint of the neck and the sinews is like observing paralysis between them. The great weapon follows with the rare and extraordinary, upon the joints, such as the legs and thighs. Between them, the physician's treatment is like thorns, and between them lies the benefit of the joints. The two-part condition involves three tendons, and among them are the large cartilages. We organize the simple for the two lower and upper, and we make the joints firm and well. What was from the firmness of the joints is based upon the absolute freedom of speech, and the need for it is from the small bones. We say: whatever was sound in its foundation for the movement of the limbs must be repeated many times in what concerns them and their totality.

[Left page - main text:]

In this matter, it is possible that it occurs in it, and from it upon it, as the compiler said — the compiler's purpose called for it. It was found to be correct, and it is confirmed to be sound, marking the center. The inferior kind: if it is made complete upon its regulation, and upon its regulation always, do not think that it fills the itch as possible, like the bandage, and the need for that. For what can be assessed from the shoulder, when it was that the bones are demanded — likewise the speech of the shoulder is thus written with desire, and with sinews having benefit — that which is most refined in the organized purified and with its surplus — the joints of it are upright, and thirty of the sound ones among the bones of the joint upon its side. Many times in what is measured, and no punishment is given, and beside it is more, for the smooth fine description of the large tendons and their articulations. Like the lower simple and the third — upon the king and its attachment — and the surplus travels from it and its neighbors, and from them are the separate and among them the other. And the surplus, and the preferred, with what is priced, and they flow, and they go, and they pass, and the best of the joints is obligatory. Its movement is made easy, and the movement is made easy by it — in the matter the completion of this is like the surplus of the kind.

[Marginalia:]
I say: when it concerns the bones and their surplus — the first chapter — and the saying of Ali on the bones and joints.

translation:
Right page:

Concerning the joints of the spine and the vertebrae: one of the two articular surfaces fits into the other. It is said that the articulation allows movement in some directions but restricts it in others, and the joint of the vertebrae together with the surrounding bones of the spinal column and its adjacent structures allows for a certain degree of bending. Right Page (Page 39):

The generated [substances] in the best position support every element that sustains them from three original roots. What was particular to the products increases among most of them, increasing gradually. When you know the science of the religious matter, which comes after arrangement, and Ahmad comes after placing knowledge of flesh upon [its proper] basis, it strengthens them. As for the lower [part], it places them and repeats them and adds what directs them to the outlets for the structure. The teeth: the flesh of the garment directs the abundance toward ease for them. It preserves among them the knowledge of what is desired.

Chapter Three: On the usefulness of the spine. Galen states that the marrow is placed to nourish it, so that it may be beneficial. What is needed for the animal [body] in its structure is derived from the benefit of the product, part of which fills it. He mentioned those who came to it and preferred it over others, noting that the original portion is [established]. A sensation of eight [units] was given until immunity was acquired, for the defects and severances were sealed. The [substance] flows through it and strengthens [the body], and after the members [are formed], the pleasant nourishment reaches the lower [region]. Together, the product after the young's nourishment, the lower [region] brings what is needed. And what comes to it and joins with the amount of the ground substance, that which came is not cold. The strengthening of the cross-substance is swift for the members, and that is its nature.

Left Page:

The benefit and vitality from some of them is the purification that gathers all knowledge from it and expends it. The parts differ among most [people], and the increase [of substance] is produced gradually. What comes to it through the religious science means what comes after arrangement, and Ahmad comes after placing knowledge of flesh upon [its proper] basis.

Chapter Three: The End Result of Teeth (in red ink):

The sweet reaches the [prescribed] time, and likewise the molars. The primary teeth and their roots replace [them], and what the children receive [as new teeth]. The girl reaches four [teeth] at each stage of growth, which grows greatly upon her. From the benefits and what is pleasant to it, and what concerns every [person who] reaches maturity. Right Page:

Conditions: Third — when it connects through the lower arm bones to reach the extremities of movement, its value is not between its two ends when connected, but rather the bone of the forearm negates that, so between its two ends is proportional to the arm. Its foundation is in joining and connection which occurs with the bone from within — not from mere adjacency but from the interdigitation between the joints. The interdigitation of the vertebrae forms the chain of suspension of the limbs; it does not act without reason, for when they seek relief from fatigue, if they are among the interdigitations, then the sound probe applies.

On the breadth of the anterior: The hollow bones at their midpoints — their cavities and hollows — may have an inferior constitution and range freely without deterioration. What is above the pure [element] and below it has a pure basis in the original possession. Whether it has a basis toward the origin of the throat or whether it relates to the upper part of the covenant, and the blood of the chains in some of them is the original soundness of the probe, honoring both of them. It is a relative quality; in the good interpreters, their ends have no benefit in them, and all those who speak and the paradise — for both of them, what I see upon them is three broad, flattened things. Therefore, when it became heavy, what was found in the members — what was among them, swift in its origin — enters into them; the longest and most supple, and the sinew, and the cartilage, and the probe clothes the bodies, directing them toward correction as their final purpose and its treatment.

Left Page:

It attaches at the nasal region, pressing on it at its base, without correction of what is within it, and for every wing there is a wing from it — an explanation — and for every one of its names there is a value not between Zaldan. The Hanafi position is between what the wing and the strong wing of the summer resorts [contain]. This occurs in its exit from that which benefits it, and what is conjoined passes through the protection of the water of the fold. Seven [matters] emerge from it — from the school of learning — and the scholars from the varieties from some perspectives make [it] three grades of arrangement, gathering [them]. It was among the breadth of the wide opening, and in its value for the purpose of its arrangement, what was in the generous nourishment — the joint between the two — and not yielding to them, repelling the Platonic [elements]. Whether it was counted among them as foreign — not being from the sweet of their training — whether it was in their discipline, it is to be disliked. Until the part toward what has settled in it, the soul — I do not find it increasing — is of the dominion, and what increases of the dominion. Behind it toward the lowly, toward the corrected — the superficial ones — and what is confirmed, which is established in the upper aspects of the features, bearing what is borne toward the bodies naturally by its acceptance from the sinews. Whether it was in some of them the ligament, and what was able to be from the pure quality of the ligament — and it was the night toward what flows from the training of the members, arranging them and ordering them — these two acquisitions upon the night toward the matter without its dome. Also, as for what began — some of them advanced it and some of them marked it — it also was for all the assemblies; it is only that the localities — from what is presented, its knowledge, given to them — from its saying toward the training of its benefit, the safest for its completion.

translation:
RIGHT PAGE:

Chapter Twenty-One: On the Anatomy of the Forearm

The forearm is composed of two large bones, joined together, arising from four tendons extending below. Their structure relates to the elbow joint below, from which the palm connects upward. They share in supporting the carpal region and work together in movement. The two bones keep a space between them, closest at the distal end near the wrist. The outer tissues wrap around them from four directions, attached firmly to the joint structures. The carpal bones articulate with the end of the forearm bones, allowing motion in all directions. The tendons from the forearm pass through the wrist into the fingers, allowing extension and flexion. The muscles that extend and flex the wrist originate partly from the outer bone and partly from the inner, giving the hand its range of motion including extension, flexion, adduction, and abduction.

LEFT PAGE:

Chapter: On the Anatomy of the Palm Muscles

The palm extends flatly when supported from below at the elbow and the armpit region. The palm spreader muscle arises from three fused bones, joined tightly, from which fibers spread into the palm. When placed flat against the ground, the bones oppose one another from below, securing the palm. The mechanism holds the four small bones in order, structured like a framework with regular proportions. The four bones align with the four fingers, providing attachment from the side facing the fingers, and tendons emerge from them spreading toward the fingers in proportion to their size. The small short bones of the carpus articulate together and support the palm mechanism. Chapter Twenty-Three: On All the Finger Joints — each bone is like the corresponding bone in other animals, similar in structure to those of other living creatures, all sharing in their form and function, varied only in proportion and kind, serving the purposes of extension, flexion, rotation, and all other movements known to occur in the fingers.

Chapter Six: On the Description of the Muscles of the Lip

As for the lip, its muscles are twelve: two come from its outer portion, four drawing from the lateral side toward the outer aspect; two from below. The lip's position has been arranged such that each of them allows for appropriate movement. Two serve to extend its substance — these are the lateral muscles — and they facilitate movement. As for the medial ones, they stretch to connect the teeth, and the third portion of the lip acts as a joint with the teeth, so that movement is made easy and smooth.

Chapter Seven: On the Description of the Muscles of the Eyelid

As for the eyelid, it has two small muscles. The first of them, which is the receiving one, attaches to the front of the eyeball; its actions pertain to the limiting and moving of the eye in all directions, whether many or few. The wisdom of its design and the nature of its path is such that it allows for spreading. Thus, by means of them, the eyelid is controlled, directing and guiding it, so that the eyelid first opens and then closes, governing the movement of both.

Note: This manuscript page is from Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb). The text is heavily damaged and partially illegible in many places. The following translation represents the legible portions, which deal with topics of joint dislocations, treatments, and related anatomical considerations.

Right page:

Concerning the coupling of some dislocations — we have already mentioned what causes this dislocation to occur in the joint. Among them is what we have palpated as the cause of what was damaged, and among them is what pertains to the parts. The cause of this is the stretching toward the joint surfaces, which require the first section. That which causes it — the first movement — passes through the branches of the joint to the first of the spine to the lower vertebra. The cause is that what flows from the dominant nature overcomes it, moving away from it. That retreating movement settles from what the sinew carries — there is no god but God — and the two receptors: the first two receiving structures support the first muscle gently. Like a traveler, it demands the opposite and seeks the difference from its approach. It is consumed, taken entirely, making the muscle move in the opposite direction, causing the joint to slip from its proper place. Three dislocations occurred, and through the anatomy of each one of them, a great cavity of the deep structure appeared. And from this, to the four parts, and what pertains to the joint surfaces — the treatment lies in taking the original approach, and through it goes what requires a joint treatment. The physician applies the first compress, and between the two sides passes the reinforcement — two joint supports. The first passage, the joint, the first — through its binding, the discourse, and the separation from the first joint — and balance.

For this reason, the administration of the medication is done with the least amount of wind. Consider that if one proceeds without deviation, between one extreme and the other there are about twenty degrees, among which two squares are defined, connected by means of the Meccan method and by addition. The organ that has no administrator for it has two squares between them, connected by means of calculation and subtraction. The considered one, having fixed the reduction, achieves satisfaction at the lowest degree. The application of the subtraction to the fine substance, for several days, and avoiding the obstacle of the constriction, is such that nothing from it escapes the densification. Concerning the formation of the ascending elements — two types — it resembles a king, and the fine and linear form of the passage. It will be at times simple and at other times complex, according to the nature of the fine substance and the reduction required by the companion of the honey. The administrator said: as for the pathway, it completes the two applications and their physician and connects them. The two pathways, between the two routes, the reduction, the remedy with the reduction, and its pair emerge from the diminisher who controls the fine substance, and from its authority, when the matter manifests, the path emerges. Every course and above it the pale reduction confirms the days of its pair from the path. The action of the pair proceeds, the least, and is associated by what is between them from the pathway of the treatise. The fine substance will be from the primary elements, from which it forms what the other pair acts upon. The two pathways come from their mixing, and when examined, our path is confirmed.

Left Page:

By this, the difference brings forth the matter of eight parts of the fine substance, of what remains of our understanding. As for the pathway, and if one is inclined to that which is like it, of which there are one hundred, in the extraction of the reduction there is half of the fundamental established substance, from which the growth emerges by the permission of God. The fine substance which belongs to the principle proceeds according to what comes to the administrator from it, with its definition and its father's. The one who has no administrator — when the matters are examined and its meaning is understood — is in a state of restriction. They are similar to the surface of the fine substance, which, when examined, reveals the constriction and its connection. They follow each other as it has been received, and the remedy attains what it has acquired according to its proper measure. It removes the light element, and when it is established, it emerges according to the pathway. It is said that similarly, the meeting point takes in proportion, and the remedy of the fine substance proceeds forward, and the best of the reduction advances pathwise. The principle, whose name is the administrator of the fine substance, emerges; if it is established as a foundation, then the natural remedy is formed. The base is the collection of the chest and the cavities, and we have learned the source of the addition. Inside the reduction there is that which is like the foundation; its condensation in both of them relates to the finest elements. The condensation, its intensity, and what God has set for it — in both of them — and what belongs to it are guided to their names. With a little of the envelope, the connection between the principle and the fine substance whose administrator is known is achieved, and after our elaboration, from the mentioned pathway, it is the preferable one.

translation:
[Right page:]
On the treatment of palpitations of the heart: know that God — may He be exalted — has placed within the heart a faculty by which it is affected by disturbances coming to it. When a rapid and violent cause encounters this sensitive faculty in a person and agitates it, then if one has not yet recovered from that, the neighboring organs are affected and the weakness spreads. This is the Syrian method: if the cause is distant from the heart, one should identify it and treat it from that direction. Look at the foundations and the basic principles, and know that the treatment of the organs nearest to the heart takes priority. The treatments and strengthening measures, and the humoral remedies — all are to be considered. The heart is to be supported and nourished, and the causes that weaken it from outside are to be removed. When the digestion is complete and the matter has ripened, then the evacuation may proceed. The compound medicines for strengthening and for evacuation are to be used according to the condition. The most noble of the members and the most worthy of preservation is the heart, and it must be given priority in treatment.

[Left page:]
The place of the beneficial and restricted medicines: among those things which are prescribed in this regard — when the condition is as described — one should proceed carefully, avoiding excess. The third aspect concerns the administration of medicines and entering gently into the treatment without abruptness, not passing beyond what is appropriate, lest harm result to the patient. One must be careful in applying the rules, for what appears mild may not be so. The humors and the temperaments play a role in what is tolerable.

Chapter Three: On the Explanation of the Ascending Vapors
The ascending vapor — its entry into the vessels draws all that is in the neighboring parts, whether from the right side or the left. Each side is considered according to its own condition and what it receives. As for the two types of Syrian vapors: one must distinguish between them in what is near and what is far. There are those vapors which enter within, and those which act from outside. The first type operates at the level of the fundamental constitution. The three categories of treatment — the internal, the external, and the intermediate — are each assigned their appropriate medicines. The compound prescriptions address both the simple and the complex conditions.

Chapter Three: On the Explanation of the Waters of the Compound Preparations
And each requires its own response.

What collects in the esophagus is a granulation and gathering of the continuous parts of the nutrient substance. From the upper passage to the lower, that which is carried from it distributes what is refined in the intestines toward the raw and undigested matter. The digestive faculty, along with its adjacent parts, works upon what passes through it from the substance of the rabbit's passage, purifying what is refined from what is contained in the great vessels of digestion, distinguishing therein all of the refined matter. The remainder follows the ascending passage from the refined matter up through the filtering channels of digestion. The sanguinous faculty distributes from it what is pure to the material, and what falls hard upon it reaches the firm bodies therein. In it also is found what descends from the remembrance of it — the attraction of digestion — ascending to the lower stations. It is mixed therein with what rises from the upper parts, concerning the balance of digestion on both sides, and the moisture thereof. The fourth gathering follows what is directed to the lower parts, settling therein between the seekers. When this is established, it attracts from the extremity of the digested material outward from the chamber. The nutriment then is presented to be absorbed from the parts through what is distributed to it, and from it passes to the whole complex of elements available to the absorbing organs. That which is refined reaches the lower vessels of the blood. As for what increases in the body's capacity, it spreads to whatever enters into the vessels, running through the flesh. The mixture of humors from the joining of the refined digested matter at its articulations is thus established.

[Left page]
As for what the digestive faculty accomplishes: it gathers and refines what is carried to the body through the lower and upper faculties together, which carry from within the chest cavity and the second direction toward the salty substances. It aligns the natural and abnormal elements, conditions the nutriment, and likens what rises through the lower channels according to what is established — namely the retention of the substance. The hearing faculty and what the heat brings in the lower part are regulated, and the lower faculty carries forward what the capacity for absorption establishes. The attracting and higher faculties adjust what passes through the channels, and the nutriment passes to its place through the body's interior. The cooling and heating faculties temper what is distributed, and the absorptive capacity in the lower and upper parts digests proportionally. The substance is carried through the vessels, and the proper humor is distributed to the members. The higher faculty distributes onward to the further reaches, and what rises from the lower passages follows the channels of the upper, each following the other in sequence, each receiving what it is given so that proper nourishment and refinement are established, and the lower sends upward through the channels in sequence, so that the faculty of the body perfects its receipt of nourishment and completes what is necessary for the members.
