The spirit and vital faculties ascend from the pylorus through a well-known path upward to the liver. From there the seminal fluid flows, drawn by its nature toward the pubic region, resting upon the hip bone. It descends to the liver from below, in the lower parts lying over the abdomen, so the fluid passes from the vessels and channels to whatever reaches the digestive organs within them. The sensation from the side of the seeker dwelling within the chambers flows, and the fluid of the white substance passes through. Among what reaches the digestive faculty is what gathers and accumulates within it, and the reason for this is that the liver retains and stores what the colon receives, and this increases and flows. The epididymis does not carry back what settles upon the conduit leading to the great organ. In the semen of the male there is benefit, and it flows into the vessel of the fluid of the two vessels. It is good when it enters through the first path, and what remains in the two vessels at that point. It precedes in the passage through the digestive organs, the male and female alike, like those before it. The fluid ascending from the second is drawn to the liver, refined by experience, and its portion is absorbed and received. It directs the passage of fluid, increases it, and spreads what God has ordained far and wide.

Left page:

The Sixth Chapter: On the nature of the chambers and what benefits the organ.

The natural faculty directs the organ, preventing whatever interrupts the passage and the flow.

Those who seek, seek according to a method that gathers from the spirit what is primary, because the natural faculty and the physician aim at the originals of what is mentioned. The master gathers according to what saliva requires, for each absence comes from within it, and from it proceeds to its end. It is urged that the effect upon the matter should require it, and what is found is in its praise. Whatever is needed of its quality and its scent appears in its outward form. The physician, however, does not simply treat with its scent by bringing it near, exposing what is unknown from these lands. Rather, that falls to the philosopher with the naturalist and the physician, if they reflect upon it, because within them lies the mentioned meaning. Whatever pertains to the meanings of the spirit — the meaning for which no sign appears — has been conveyed from medicine to the physicians, as if from what is said, left to the philosopher to address. The second chapter on the natural meanings of the new [matters]: as for the natural spirit, it has its definitions, its collective properties, and the means by which one comes to know it in the body. The natural [faculty] from every direction, concerning its benefits, its characteristics, its evidence and what leads into it, as found in the meadow [i.e., the field] of the body.

Left page:

The matter itself: as for what is suitable, it rises to the land. By extending the natural faculties upon the foundations of nature, what is blessed in its circulation is known and understood. What is constant and what is transient, and what is given — the permitted — is shared by those who are assigned to it. Those who settle in their place and withdraw, what was intended from the analysis was not found other than what was, and thus it was. The two faculties, the compound and the simple, are present in the field of the stars: what was hoped for and what is near, and what is distant proceeds from what is built. The strong one held over those who preceded it, gathering the demands and settling, marking that affair accordingly. And if it was measured, the amounts were determined by time in successive states, and it was seen from among the merits of that distance upon the philosopher, the judge, and the corrector — the healer proceeding to set right the general matter. The received opinions, mixed with what the senses convey from the essential and the universal, resembling the images, arrive at that. Being present in the knowledge of the ways, hearing in the knowledge of what is transmitted — now and before — leading to what is reached. This achieved opinion, it is not possible without acceptance of views, specializing as it was in the foundation. The analogies and similarities, and showing this result at its root, rejecting the inferior — sharing from every direction, concerning its benefits and its characteristics and what leads into it, as found in the field of the genus, arriving at last.

translation:
Right page:

On substitution and repletion: what resembles the non-existent — this is the action of the dying faculty. It is said that what is praised and what follows in the categories of genus is the first principle. In the similar parts, in every organ among them, above the pulpit of that which resembles — if it differs from what resembles it, the faculty is directed only through the body without restraint from the liver. We perform an action resembling the general — and as for the faculty of the king, it causes prevention and withholding from it, drawing toward the faculty of the retreating part, organ by organ, for the reason described. The bone, the tongue, and the like belong to those things similar in constitution. What is suitable through this faculty — it is directed toward the first desired natural faculty. What is established by it — when the organs are aligned, in their two forms, in their expansion and contraction, their capacities accommodating, being shared by it — the limbs and the stated faculties — then as it recedes, it is drawn toward the faculty of election in that which is refined, related to the following faculty and its attendants.

Chapter Three: On Natural Temperament

The faculty in the composite body is served by the faculty of nutrition, preventing harm, as the faculty of attraction works. What draws and holds — the attracting faculty, the retaining faculty — then what is sought is a hindrance and an effect. That which acts with speed upon what is demanded brings about restraint upon the faculty.

Left page:

What diverts this verified faculty — what the retentions bring and what is separated from that — is like assistance for the participants. When what is retaining it is released, the attracting and holding faculty is settled and subdued. This is the chapter on the faculty that is evident from it: it leads to what is proper for restoration, except that which belongs to action in this matter. In what restricts and in what grows from it and its foundations — and as for what is surplus in the faculties, what enters into it from the shared and drawing parts — it is also among the faculties that govern what is retained: if the retainer is absolute, then if the constitution is established by swelling — if the retainer is delicate, then this action is sound, leading to proper constitution and rectification. Upon this, what arises and what the surplus brings is refined in what governs. What is left over is either surplus or is measured — and what is taken from it is dispensed with. From its use in attracting and drawing, the surplus is directed. The shared matters — what is drawn from it — are retained in their proper holders. The adjacent and the neighboring: if it draws and if there is an enclosure and a veil, the surplus faculty is purified, the faculty is distributed, prevention occurs, and the faculties emerge. Nature in its entirety with all its terms — the first of those — with its capacities enumerated, with marrow and medicine — the nature resembles the animal in its entirety, shared for the physician, with marrow and medicine — this we understand.

translation:
Right Page:

These qualities that are dissolving — since coldness is what issues from the clothes and covers — apply to all temperaments. As for the dissolved [humor] and blood, those are the dominant temperaments. The alert faculty, in its least form, is individual in its absolute form, gathered, thinner, finer, and lighter. These are the separating movements and their filling functions — whatever the retentive faculty draws of excess, it conveys to the attracting and composing [faculty]. From each of the heavy and cold qualities, once they have moved away and been fortified by that which strengthens them, the retentive faculty holds them within itself. The attractive faculty is complex, drawing from what overcomes it, going to the [organ's] structure — this is its gift to the parts. The expulsive faculty acts upon what is received, dispatching it outward when diseased, extracting from it what belongs to it. The retentive faculties — the two holding powers — along with the attracting faculty, cause the passive matter to remain, acting upon it in the domain of dryness. These things, by the nature of motion, cause the carrier of the nutritive faculty to act upon them. Naturally, when it [the pneuma] flows in its course and direction, the retentive faculty seeks out the natural passages; and when it is settled, it remains.

Left Page:

It is established that the active and passive [faculties] must work together — the retentive faculty acts upon them in a manner befitting it. The coldness and the external coldness, along with what it contains of residence in the retentive faculty — if this continues for a period, the faculty of the body, spread through the retentive [channels], causes the humors to flow toward the passages and joints and places, dispersing upward. The faculty settles into its category and the colors become clear among them — what is the quality of that place? The retentive faculty uses what is stable, directing it to what is established in the attracting faculty — this is the memory of that. Its surfaces cover the areas of land and elevation, from where it overflows, compressing the channels. The faculty settles into it, and the united [forces] serve whatever the faculty summons — the layers, the repulsive and attractive forces, and the joints. Like the winds of the house — if the retentive faculty has that [quality], it acts upon the matter therein. The settling of layers and their movement: whatever enters the attracting faculty causes motion and produces from it its portion. The nutritive and the passive [faculties] — the attracting force is the carrier of motion, broadly acting, causing its effects. The retentive faculty — for it is the opening that expands the retentive [matter], establishing the sediment and the remainder, the fine and the excess — is what is known. The proximate [faculty] with the retentive vessel settles into its seat, gathering toward the retentive place.

Marginal note: No elevation and above the faculty.

translation:
Right Page:

Regarding summer: it produces certain harmful vapors from the times of day that generate [various conditions]. As for its regulation, one must reduce exposure during the hottest part of the day, taking care throughout the prolonged season. The causes attributed to this relate to the organs and how they draw moisture toward vital channels. All of these flow toward the digestive pathways and facilitate the movement of humors through the body, directing the liquids and solids of the passages through the body.

Regarding the moist temperament: if the constitution is of this nature, the humors become distributed and the body is susceptible to ulceration and inflammation. For young persons with sensitive constitutions, the organs are stimulated and affected by the conditions of the season. This is the manner in which conditions of the organs arise, affecting the young especially. Their treatment requires washing and administering appropriate medications, ensuring proper digestion and management of their humors. The second phase brings further complications affecting the entire bodily system. The royal physician must examine the amount of discharge and determine if the situation is manageable or requires intervention. The flow from the organs must be checked, and the cause of any excessive discharge must be determined. The faculty governing digestion must be supported, and medications that regulate the flow must be given. The humors must be managed in the remaining seasons.

Chapter on the Four Seasons and the Animal Faculties.

Left Page:

As for the vital spirit and its nature, it is filled with its power, and when it settles in the organs, it produces diverse vapors. The lungs and heart draw these inward, and the various types of faculties attributed to them facilitate this. The refined product generated therefrom is what is drawn by the subtle faculty from its sources, and the vital faculty then acts upon it repeatedly, refining it further. This faculty governs the movements of all the organs collectively, and through the opposite faculty it controls sensation and movement, leading to what arises in the body. The nerves are subsequently affected by this, and the cause of death is what disrupts this faculty. The soul and its power, if deprived, lead to paralysis and related conditions. Protection from these conditions is sustained as long as God preserves the movement of the spirit and its faculties remain intact.

translation:
On the faculties that govern the lateral parts of the body, and likewise every organ that exists on each side — this is due to the faculties among them. When the soul as a whole proceeds from the entirety, then even if it is the primary product, it serves no purpose in the lateral faculties of the primary side unless it is established without distress and functions accordingly in each part. Thus the faculty ascends and is estimated according to all the general principles derived from it, as if the essence of these faculties remains and persists through them, activating the movement of the joint. The natural soft faculty encompasses all its components — its extent and breadth — and the faculty works upon the most excellent things. It is as if the healthy living force benefits fundamentally, the physical elements moving toward the actions of the many. This is indicated by the resemblance of the good nature of this thing to what is intended — for the faculties of the remaining transient things lose their orderliness and natural state, and two rulings follow. This is established when the soul connects and the bodily elements extract from it everything of an earthy nature, and all things proceed in their proper course between them, as they were, reaching their perfection. The faculties act upon the blending and tempering thereof, and it is as if the good faculties are thus established.

On the right side: The faculty, as established by its statement of action — and likewise the third of the isolated faculties — does not allow this pattern of the distant to stimulate that faculty. When the faculty of a given member is established and the speech of this matter is stimulated, and when examined from the perspective of that member in terms of what it learns in the noble field of what leads to it and what comes from it — toward death, and even if the diminishing faculty proceeds from some of its sources and the senses and the rest — then it would be established by the speech of the good for it to be possible, except that the other relief is general. It is perceived in terms of what brings benefit and in terms of what the speech produces as an onset of convulsion. When convulsion occurs, it occurs before the fluids reach it, and the faculties are not as they were for the first essence. The first distinction is that it establishes the faculties so that all convulsion is not what the physicians consider — that the faculty is held in the brain, grasping it at first in the direction of the tongue. And if the faculty from the brain proceeds to what purifies it, then it does not benefit, because the faculty present in it cannot receive it — and likewise in the liver and in the human being. The physicians who employ treatment of convulsion directed to the brain in the course of receiving it — and the sensation and pain at the first level — but whether it be in the liver or whether it be the primary product — [the first].

translation:
Right page:

Every faculty that issues forth from what it issues from runs according to its strength. If this is supported, it guides it. It relates to the faculties that physicians call the natural physician. As for the natural faculty, it is named as such because whenever it is present, it produces a fundamental result. Together with its natural healing capacity, it precedes the description of qualities and conditions. The natural faculty, when it acts through the movement of humor, operates through the perceptive faculties. These faculties include: those that pertain to awareness, those related to beneficial knowledge, and the natural faculty which is called the latent faculty.

CHAPTER FIVE: THE ANALOGOUS FACULTIES

The analogous faculties occupy two positions in the body, serving it in various ways. Just as the perceptive faculties work in the external senses, so too are the perceptive faculties located in the internal domain. The perceptive faculties in the interior of the body, which are like the external sensory faculties, gather at a single faculty after the individual organs, when they are located at the root of impression from the external faculties. The function of perception is combined from this, because its cause in this act is what resembles the faculties working for each sense. Among the analogous faculties are those related to breath, resembling the taste and smell faculties in their subtle workings.

Left page:

Regarding what dominates in the judgment, which is what is called the common sense among physicians and scholars, and which the natural philosophers call the receiver of all that comes to it from individual sensibles — this faculty retains what dwells within bodies and preserves the forms. The natural science of intrinsic knowledge is that which holds together the subtle faculties and works upon the various types. However it is composed, it resembles what is derived from primary matter and the natural disposition. The faculty that physicians speak of — when its origin is sound and its nature complete — the natural analogous faculties receive the impression of what comes to them from bodies, and when the natural faculty acts upon them it defines and perfects them, taking from them what it takes. Thus all of the faculties of both types — the practical and the theoretical — work together. When matter is prepared through analogy and form is combined into it and shaped, it becomes built upon what appears from the compound in the finest of forms. That which is produced from these two represents their composition, moving from what is natural to what lies within. These are the faculties of the internal perceptive powers — the evident and the latent — acting through the whole.

It may be that what is called the condition occurs as a drum-like swelling or as heat. When it comes only from a single cause, it may happen that all matters come together and the underlying cause is established. When the cause is a deficiency in the basic constitution, then we observe all the varieties of that condition. The primary basis is that which accumulates in the first stages and increases, so that what the Galenic physicians describe becomes evident — namely the compound and simple varieties, which carry known names and types. Most practitioners recognize from the known types how to classify them. When they gather in the joints, they work upon the hearing and the nearby structures, and certain practitioners have noted this. The first matter is that it must repel what has settled flat, and the body must regulate the body's general order. When the judgment is near its limit and the errors are subtle, and the resolution of what is dissolved is complete — as for what is sent to the appropriate place — then as for the first of the watery humors, it may be that they originate as either a simple or a compound, prevailing by temperament. And some of them come from deposits of hardness and cancer, and related to them are the glandular structures in which the calcified and hardened deposits develop along with the flesh and marrow. And among the species of the glandular tissue, the individuals of these glands congregate together.

Left page:

The liver conditions — the greenish humor — are like a sultan commanding the body: they seize upon what is like a lump within it. They persist and continue to draw the nutrients, with the superfluities and the tendons involved. The cancer and the hardness, when they intensify and settle, lead to an inability of the body to repel them. The pain does not increase, and the cancer causes something resembling a disability in the limbs. It is known that what the humor does is to dissolve the part and make its nature null, just as the cancer does. It is also known that the separation between the liver's dissolution and the hardness and adjacent nodes follows from its own nature. The resemblance to hardness comes especially in the blood conditions, which resemble what flows toward the part. As for what accompanies the accumulation of matter, it gradually increases little by little, until the separation grows and spreads, and it becomes possible to palpate the mass. Then in time the competition of the humors diminishes and the dissolution of the compacted matter begins. The soft, gentle, and pliable forms are those contained within the coverings of the body; they tend in some cases to take on certain colors. Know that the watery and mucous humors differ from the mixed, and taken together they vary in presentation.

Right page:

When the echo of moisture reaches it and connects with it in a manner that prevents it from passing through the channels as we have described regarding the cause of the humors — if not all of the distinguishing factor is carried, the quest for what benefits it is sought by its name. At that time, the temperament of the day is determined by that which produces excess in the wind through the mixture of the superfluity, replacing the arrival of the moisture. The wind is present in humans and its effect is repelled from it, and this is because the elderly need it before its arrival to be cold. When it inclines toward its nature and the wind overwhelms and seeks to block every path, preventing its flow, and substitutes for it so that its passage through is prevented and directed elsewhere, and the superfluity of wind is eliminated and the moisture is checked — then the wind's temperament prevents the superfluity from reaching its natural state, and its natural temperament is altered. All the natural substances and their superfluities thus seek their proper path through each treatment.

Chapter Three: On the Natures of the Seasons

Know that the four seasons, according to physicians, are understood by scholars to have four natures.

Left page:

At the time of the analysis, the foundational principles of the Canon are considered in each quarter. From its basis, what is established is that the quarter's nature — which leaves no difficulty — is as follows: whenever the moisture is reduced from the cold, or increased with warmth, it remains so always. Its natural course keeps it in balance according to the natural temperament. The superfluity is classified from the signs, and the correction is the fundamental object in the chapter on the temperate. It is permitted in external matters from the weakest degree of mixture, and the humors are gathered together. The eight external types together constitute the wondrous, and they are grouped into eight, and spring and autumn share equal parts. The standard of the seasons, or rather each single unit, is divided into the parts of the days within its time. This is known from the signs and the indications that clarify the times. In summer, its temperament of wind and moisture is parallel to its counterpart and opposite. The interior and its specifics are like the natural faculty of the organ. The analysis of the natural moisture corresponds to spring and its heat increases the sun's effect incrementally. With each treatment one seeks to address what is needed, and in summer the matter is exacerbated. The sharp and sudden matters settle in the humors, and their trace upon the constitution remains.

translation:
Right page:

On the reasons for the wisdom in certain dietary matters concerning air and water: It has been said by Abu Bakr that when the physician disputes the conditions of moisture and the need for nourishment, one should eat one day at a time. The physician should reflect that if one habitually eats from the earth's produce in its dry season, it diminishes the excess of the natural constitution. The noble physician has indicated that the moderate temperament should be preserved, and this is the example of the aging person. The fundamental principle is that the physician should clarify the qualities of water as the physician sees fit. When the governing authority entrusts this matter to us, these are the conditions by which we abide: that the provinces and regions receive proper administration, and that the mentioned climates are accounted for. Air is given its due consideration, for it is air that sustains life. The proper functioning of the body depends on maintaining balance. The conditions of the believers in the various lands show us that when bodily imbalance occurs, the general constitution suffers. Medications that prevent harm are prescribed, and travel may be required. One should act with subtlety and wisdom, seeking what is beneficial and judicious in these matters.

Left page:

On the diseases that arise from what the physician reads and prescribes: how the earth's diseases are countered, and what is found in the elevated regions among the natural sciences and medicine. One should not be ignorant of what has been compiled regarding thick and dense substances found therein. It is necessary to examine the properties of the physician's remedies and how they relate to the treatment of rocky regions. Among those who practice medicine and observe the temperate constitutions and hidden latent conditions, one must study what comes from the earth and understand its properties. Among the cold remedies, some are more effective than others in treating certain conditions. The physician's knowledge must be well-grounded. One should sit and deliberate, having noted all the necessary conditions of health and temperament. The physician must consider the natural constitution and guide the patient toward balance. The learned physician must build upon fundamental principles and arrive at sound conclusions. The noble physician should not deviate from these scientific principles. The treatise concludes that the physician must complete his knowledge of natural science, accepting the moderate path, following the course of sound treatment, and adhering to the established principles of medicine and its proper classification.

translation:
Right page:

Regarding its cause — when conditions and related factors occur after a period of mild temperament, such that fine, subtle moisture is called upon, and the matter approaches — what is near the absolute in the two qualitative dimensions — the basis from which nutrition derives — the light and gentle [temperament] prevails alongside the great cities. It has been said that [the physician] must attend to the subtle quality of [the season], carrying the moisture of the air and what proceeds from it — which is what the humours call upon. The intensely cold [quality] and likewise the intensely moist will, when they seize the water [of the body], cause harm. The accumulated cold water and what is exposed to it draws together all cold and chilled water, rendering the prolonged [disease] extensive. The most inhabited [regions] benefit from the cold wind blowing after the [autumn], for in the autumn, the cold reaches the body and the chest in particular. Autumn and the period between it and what follows: know that the difference in seasons is a cause for every type of disease, and it is fitting for the good physician to recognize this in every case — to be prepared and attentive to the causes, their effects, their harms, and their benefits. The first and most excellent [advice] is to note the actions of the climates and temperaments. Whatever is pure and whatever is combined — understand what is pure and what is combined and how they are related.

Left page:

Chapter: On the Rules of the Seasons and What Pertains to Each Season.

Among the [features] of a sound temperament is that when the temperament of the air shifts, unless some deviation from the proper balance occurs — weakening the balance through half-measures — then every excess of temperament, when the opposing humour is drawn out, produces a triple discharge. And what comes from it in a balanced way is like a strengthening force, something that came to pass as a result of the encounter — refined and light for the body, acting as a moderator. The foods and drinks appropriate to the season refine and lighten the temperament. The mixtures and natural constitutions follow the cycle of the season and adjust the fine temperament, so that the physician may correct the imbalances — for the seasons continually revolve and their effects govern what the body eats and absorbs. What is drawn first is like a vessel: the primary [humour] acts upon what follows it and guides the stronger [element] to what the constitution seeks. But one must consider the place, the limbs, the joints, the water, its qualities and benefits, and each organ specifically. translation:
(Right page):

Quince benefits by correcting the wind (flatulence), it calms the wind, and its action is beneficial in the first degree and strengthens digestion. It is of cold and dry temperament, it firms and strengthens the bladder and prevents urinary incontinence. Among its properties is that it strengthens and nourishes the body and benefits the extremities. Among its uses for travelers and those in foreign lands, it helps in the healing of wounds. It helps prevent urinary flow and excess of urinary fluids, and it benefits the skin. It suits a moist temperament and corrects thick and corrupt humors. As for thick and corrupt air, when it enters the body, the corruption of the humors and the murkiness of the body result. It purifies corrupt air and thick air, for thick corrupt air when breathed into the body causes harm. The corrupt and moist air produces dampness in the body and causes the appearance of stars and constellations (i.e., spots). Among its properties is that it benefits the chest and the respite from coughing and phlegm. When used with vinegar it benefits the digestion of food and helps with excess wind. In matters of digestion and the treatment of humors, when used properly it governs the correction of excess humors. Its essence is gentle, its nature is temperate, and it carries color.

(Left page):

Do not be deceived by the appearance of things; know that when a substance is pure and clear, it mixes well with food and assimilates easily. The stomach digests it and it blends with the humors. It is useful for those whose stomachs produce excess fluids. It strengthens the womb in matters of digestion and acts within the body. When God wills, seeking His aid, it treats ailments of summer, dizziness, and wind-related diseases. God has made it beneficial in its natural properties. It is gentle and warm in temperament, and when taken in measure with a dry constitution it relieves flatulence. It settles the corrupt air within the chest and relieves discomfort. Among its beneficial properties is that it corrects the vices of the body and prevents harm. It benefits the teeth in their natural function and relieves wind. It purifies the essential minerals present in the body and corrects imbalances. Among its properties is that it strengthens the body and aids digestion, preserving its goodness and wholesome qualities.

The benefit of friction and rubbing the body with a material of fine texture has been established by those who have practiced it. Among the best of these materials are fine linen, and the first among grains is wheat. The emollients and softening agents are among the finest for smoothing and softening the skin. Were it not for the emollients and for the substances that relax the fibers, all ailments arising from different temperaments of the body would be difficult to treat. Among the conditions it benefits are: pain of the joints, pain of the entire body, roughness of the natural constitution, thirst, and all of these together. It has been noted that when one is treated in summer, the treatment should be moderate, and likewise the regimen of the patient should be observed. In the early stages of summer, one should begin with light treatments, and when conditions warrant, the mixtures of treatment should be balanced. The acts of the physician in treating by natural methods demand care. One should know that the darkest and most extreme remedies should be used only when necessary. The regulations differ between summer and winter, and after practice, the physician will understand what is appropriate for each season.

[Left Page]

If the condition is present and arises from water, particularly when mixed with certain substances that cause looseness, and if its temperament has been altered, then the physician must seek to treat the ailments. In treating through nourishment, one should know that certain foods cause wind and flatulence, and one must balance what is consumed. The regimen of the physician is to distinguish among ailments and to treat the body according to its needs. Among the conditions requiring treatment are those of dry and moist temperament, and one must account for hearing and balance in treatment. If the wind is of a dominant nature, and the patient has a certain constitution, then the treatment must be adapted accordingly. And when the conditions are such, the treatment of chickenpox and measles requires that the pigmentation of the body return to normal. Among the internal ailments, there are those that require specific treatments, and the physician must know that in summer the treatment differs from that in winter, and the regimen must be adapted accordingly. These ailments and their treatments have been established, and the physician must know what is appropriate for each season and each constitution.

Some of the physicians have omitted certain matters, perhaps because the cause was unclear to them, or they sought to abridge. translation:
Left Page (folio 114):

Concerning what is done with the beetles [cantharides/blister beetles]: its cause is what we have described — when its effect is to harm, there is a spreading [of the poison] and it becomes absorbed into the body. What is gathered toward the strong [constitution] — one must know the properties [of the remedy]. If it was administered, one should not use it except that armor [defense] was known to them, and some of these [effects] come from above. The eastern [wind] causes no effect except through [its] properties, acting upon what is natural from the subtle [elements]. Let it be noted in the places [of treatment] that the countries have their people, and the local character fills [the remedy]. Its nature is aided by its companions, and these are drawn toward [the remedy], and they gather this in what is desired.

Chapter Nine:
On the difference between ambergris and its similar and natural counterpart — the ambergris varieties.

Some of these [preparations] settle, and the companions in the way of what is found — what is not helped, and there is no companion in [the treatment]. As for what is found in the way of the pure [remedy], it is established with the humors, and [one should know] that it does not happen because of its nature. Then it must be lessened in the [amount of] blockages, and half [must be taken] — and it is from those [remedies]. Its cause: the most stable, the most noble — the first basic [compound] — and if that is the case, then for it is the compound [remedy]. And if it were distributed in the four [humors] in measure, and if it were possible and settled, then it should be [made] smooth. And for every [remedy] one should draw from the simple [compound], so that it does not go to the lowest [stage] in which it lies hidden.

Right Page:

For as long as [the physician] wishes it to be in a [certain] state, and for a [certain] condition — the great tablet [remedy]. What is in it does not harm, for the totality [of the remedy] is [contained] within it, and not [otherwise]. Upon [the patient's] good health [it acts], building upon it and upon what is indicated and what is most appropriate. And what is refined from the compound [remedy] — as is [measured] from the coagulated [element], when administered. The eastern [constitution] — indeed, for every [compound], not but [acting upon] what is coagulated and what is moist [in temperament]. The way of the treatment and the handling of people of the same kind — the sun [warms] all things and it requires [appropriate] temperament, and from every country. What is drawn from it — the most refined [element] — to draw out the thing and its requirement — except for [the eastern] direction. And some of them [indicate] the highest [remedy] with the hands of God — but [pointing to a] direction [of treatment]. The [qualified] ones with what is refined — three [types] of [compound remedies] are the well-known long [preparations] from the most refined [compounds]. And the simple [remedy] is as far [removed] as the noble from the compound — and if they were all thus, toward the closest [remedy], following [the method]. The second: that the ruling [properties] and the mixture in the countries [vary] in their rulings. Another [consideration] is [what occurs] in Basra in [certain] countries: we [used to] trade in the southern [goods] — there, if it was [found] — then the southern [quality] refines the southern [element], and it passes over [the body] according to [its] effect upon the extent [of illness]. And the path is drawn from the south [when] if it was [found], one considers [its] measure and extent. And what remains [is] raised — as [the physician] sees fit — a just [amount] — and what follows from it is an extract for the lowest [organs].

Right page (folio recto):

كان فيه أمر بحاوذ وإفادن لأن فيه الغالب الطم فلم ألم طدي فمعن
سحيل سحيمون الى الداه كأن تلنا المظلم قدبعين فيصيل جمعون البها

translation:
Right page:

We place at the mouth of the bladder the thickened passage of the bladder, so that what passes through it is only what the retaining barrier allows to pass through, concerning what passes into the true exit of the air from the essential matter. Those who verify this and among the most refined of those who filter it in this world are those who contend with it from their spinning, and we interpret this for what it is worth.

Whatever one says about it, its nature is such that if the dominant quality in it overwhelms the digestion, then it becomes difficult to dissolve it, bringing together the obscure matters. Whenever the air advances toward the front and produces condensation of the qualities and sharpness, it blocks the passages. And concerning what befalls from the passage of the cold air into the kidneys, and what results from it, including discharge and diarrhea — this is because the cold air penetrates the tissues and corrupts the natural order of the organs.

When it dries up the moisture, it prevents constriction, and blocks the subtle passages. The body becomes weakened in its digestion and in the expulsion of phlegm and produces harm. In the chest, the wind falls and creates griping in the stomach, and the complexion becomes altered, causing the humors to be disrupted, and with that comes harm to the digestion.

Left page:

Color acts upon the complexion through the alteration of the mixture, affecting the heart and the senses, regulating the humors by means of what directs the flow toward the interior. It is useful for those of cold and inverted temperaments, for those with cold and dry constitutions, and it refines the air, bringing about moisture in the body.

When air is transferred to the interior, the body becomes free from sediment, and the air acts upon the organs restoring balance. When the mixture is excessive, it causes the digestion to deteriorate, and the organs become overwhelmed. Dwelling in it causes moisture to be excessive, altering the humors in various ways depending on the cause and the distance from pure air and good weather.

When the wound heals properly and the color and strength are restored, the organs become refined. We have mentioned the types of primary treatments, how air descends into the proper channels in a suitable manner. Corresponding to this, whatever refines the air and strengthens the stomach and prevents griping, stimulates the natural temperament, purifies the intellect, and benefits the lungs.

translation:
[Right page]

Blessed be Lutf Allah ibn Mubarak

As for wealth, the southern aspect carries the favorable qualities toward the inner pattern. The base of perception is the lowest opening, and that has been written because the matter flows from the responses. The actions of corruption and diseases affecting it include the tributaries of the outlet, among them the settled and the constant. The first age and the intake of nourishment for the body, love, and the chest, and one cannot sit in the category of the southern type, governed by the movement of analogies. It resembles the lateral aspects, and it is like joy, and diseases are recognized and classified. The spirit and happiness produce itching and the ripening of corruption, and they draw forth the teeth and they creep. The grains are indeed not fortified in the best of salt in generosity of salt.

On Eastern Remedies:
These treatments sprout from the latter part of the water and what it produces and directs, with gentleness and softness. It arises by the grace of gentleness — what sprouts toward the latter part of the day. The water and the dew of the eastern and the eastern aspects attract the grain from the herbs.

On Western Remedies:
Among the breezes, what is in toward the water and the daytime — from its knowledge above the sun, it softens without extremity and without dryness in the water and the whole. The matter and the difference of the soul in the treatment produce redness among the causes of the temperaments of the regions — as we have mentioned in the chapter on the questions of the people of the places and what pertains to them.

[Left page]

Blessed be Lutf Allah ibn Mubarak

If one also comes to it, it is as though the one present has managed the latter, having walked it — that some seek and some disperse it. The rulings of the regions: one calls upon the example of the place, and the mixture serves the observers — the causes for their heights and their halves within themselves and their shade, and from that is extracted the condition of their environments — their dampness, their water sources, their qualities, and the abundance of water diminishing it. Wealth, water, what grows from the soil, what the land provides, what is sold and traded and given — and from these come the causes, both from themselves and from others, from here and from the mountains, each with its own quality. According to what is said, the body: everything that hearing conveys to the cold — when it is given the warmth of dates — then if the seeker among them is gentle and proper, it is furnished with lawful things and the backs of their fathers, in such a place. The hearts are settled and the souls are content, separated now by dwelling.

For the sought dwelling:
Every demon is a company, composed of its portion for the mouth — as if its nobility is this sought one. What comes quickly from movement — it is as though God has placed, in judgment, profit from the Romans. In its ground and above, the mountains with fullness of people, the movement and the approach — bringing together the people of such a place in movement. And their enclosures and above, with the mountains of perfection and approach — bringing together the people of that place, its inhabitants in movement.

On Cold Dwellings:
The cold dwellings, the cold dwellings — with vapors and especially dampness — as though if their people of the mountains walk, they walk the outskirts of the villages. The joints grow weak, and those dwelling there become weaker, and the cold dwellings further weaken their inhabitants.

text:
Right page (verso):

المحنات لبني الجلود سبع المها الاسمنة في رياستهم ولا يجيز صفهم سديدًا
ولا يرد سامه ولا كثيرهم المحنات المؤمنه والأبيها ولا يعرف الله
من الجص والاسير ويكن في البابس وكملها لفت روح ولا تفن فالعلم
وكثيرهم الأصبع فالملاكي لبابه البا كأن بمرض لاحجاجها
ان يلسمن ويفعل خلودم وبلصون وبلد ادسمتهم الين ويكون
سيهم أنه دسناثيهم ماردًا فالملاكي الثالثه سكان الملاك
العاليه أصبها أوبما الطلاد الأعبار دليليا كأولتا الثمان
سكنا الأعواد ريكوُنون دأيما في وينهم كين وباه عيروا وده ويخصوص أن

يكونت بلادهم رديجيه وأدام الملكم أبيا والبيها رطبيه فاذابت

Left page (recto):

وكذلك ألبحث منه الإجاج هاذه البلاد
فالملاكي الغربيه هذه البلاد
سند لحروما ودا لاسمتيا أنزلهاجه الأسقاطلاسند فيما ما
في التليه نايبونه فصلان التطليه الطوليه لا أعلادنا كان يساقيها ولا فهل قال
ثغورالملكين أعدلها ان كانت جنيبه منه فالمسند فالملاكي الثالثه
هذه الملاكن في أحكام البلاد الفصول أله كأترها الملاك منها أرض
أحمل الشرع يكنت الملاط كيجمعه فيها بمنطق من صنصاتها جوده الهضم
ويطلبوا أبيها الملاد فيكتب أن الأبناد لكن فالملاك ثقاطلا الملاك لهضم الرفيق
ما ما الأصبع فيما لابرض صحه باطيهم وقدود القم النفس البريات
ناريه يركن فيها في البالن أسيبوكين ومنع رما الوجه في
البالم لكي لم يوجده دأياهم وأبيهم وصائج سببًا وحيها ولشهها بلنكه
لاركن لكن عليهم سيبته بعض ملاط نيكون وكملهم لأبستين يصل
اسمعها أقلاطن كوا أنا لطمأن أن طمأنون لأسليا لكا فا الملاك ولكن واعدها
سبل وبختى قنلك كلت ما لا لواد أولاني لأن ماركم شمرعن بيبته وهذا
خلاف ما أشا ومن الملاكي الملهثته وبلواته وما لسند أد حراثتهم ودار
الفريتيه وبساوم وأسمض فتأور ومن زيده لأبواب لملك البرك ما مناخه
translation:
Right page:

The trials of the children of the cold climates are seven: their leaders are moderate in their rule and do not lead their ranks astray, nor do they reduce their number. The believers and their notables are known, and God is recognized among the imprisoned and the captive. Their spirits remain and do not perish in knowledge. Many of them are given to the fourth kingdom — the inhabitants of the high regions, those of the northern climes. They dwell in their highlands always, protected from the harsh winds, and it was customary for them to accompany one another for their reasons. The fourth kingdom of the hidden war: they know their world in summer, in places that are inclined toward the south, facing the sun, mixed with good nature, and they are diligent among them. Among them is sharpness of mind and skill in crafts. As for the noble and repentant kingdom: the inhabitants of the mild, temperate kingdom, their land is cold by nature, and their lands are poor, and their king's waters are thin and moist, so when it melts...

Left page:

Likewise, the inquiry into the matter of these western lands — these lands are listed and noted, descended in what lies therein. In the third kingdom: these kingdoms fall under the rulings of the lands and their seasons, and the climate affects digestion. They seek their lands and note that the sons of the land — the climate promotes good digestion. As for summer, the land does not accept health in those who dwell there, and the soul's nature is fiery. They reside in those valleys, preventing the face from showing. They are not secure in their reasons, and among them the climate stabilizes toward moderation. This is contrary to what is found in the other climates and their territories, and those who dwell among them in the border regions and their roads, and among the gates of the kings whose breezes...

أشك تنخرنهن اختبار المأدة مضدع العروق التي في نواحي الصدر والبطن

تشرب وفرعه من مثل أمر الكتب وها في البنية نحبض وذعله الأسمر
تسمطن في الملاء كتره أمر المهم واسطل المضر الرباء التخلاف
الله بر والبأبس وبالولد الطيل البنيم المطالع والله الكيات بر ذو

(Right page)

We have said that the omission of that is a sound indication that the air in that place is as described. It is as though the members are never shed, and the seasons produce their cycles more than once. What causes miscarriage is most often the cold, the heaviness of the atmosphere, and the congestion of stagnant cold air preventing penetration. The two moistenings apply here too, and in this town in particular the varieties of air are like those of the sky. It is as though the souls dissolve, and the harmful airs in it likewise cause wasting and dryness. One must examine the vessels in the regions of the chest and abdomen. How the emptying from the first stage, as has been described, causes pressure on the hypochondriac muscles when the convulsions are severe, indicating the flow of water and the descent of the liver and spleen — these are among the signs that arise at the onset. When the air becomes humid, all the rulings of the lands and humors apply, and all the conditions of the body form within it. Its dissolution and its cure lie in the fact that its constitution purifies, since the south wind acts upon the blood and humors of bodies, drawing them through all the members quickly, and whatever is weak among them is hastened and worked upon. Weakness also comes from indigestion and from the corruption of summer and its disorders.

(Left page)

It is imbibed from its branches and the like, as the books describe, and from it the bodily constitution absorbs moisture, and the excess heat of the air prevails with its great abundance, and the damage of the alternating seasons. God the Provider and the Gentle One — the children are born and the bodies are spread about, and saliva and mucus and phlegm and digestion and assimilation all work together, and what is taken away goes to nourish what is subtle and what moves to the place of honor among the fine elements. The sublime moves toward the place described. This subject as outlined is sound in its foundations, and the air is gentle in its nature, refined, from the outset. The descriptions and conditions we have set down are such that if they are subtle and refined they transmit to the good town its rulings — what its heavens hold and what its constitution allows — and just as the ancients gave similar rulings, we say that the air softens and dries. Rather, we leave it to its natural coarseness, since we have sent it toward the fourfold city in its proper aspects and breadths. The rulings of its filled and pleasant constitution hold. The air and what is produced by it is like the air of the book — the whole of it remaining as a remainder.

translation:
Right page:

As for the precious medications, the books necessarily indicate that those who travel through various regions and lands will find that what benefits one country's people may not suit another's constitution and temperament. Therefore, one should not impose upon the inhabitants of a cold region the same remedies given to those of a hot region. Each climate has its own character, and one must pay special attention to the air of the earliest seasons.

On the Qualities of Place and Climate:
We say that places differ according to their waters, plants, and soils, and in their lands and locations, their air and breath. Vegetation, trees, and soils all vary. Consider the qualities of the soil and its moisture, the cold mountainous regions and their meadows, and the differences in health and disease among the inhabitants. The nature of the air, the openness of the land, its springs and outlets — all of these shape the temperament of those who live there. What mixes with the water, the air and its qualities — all these are factors. The pure, refined, and pleasant air is most beneficial.

Left page:

We have explained the matter of air and place at length, and shown how many conditions arise from them. Chapter Nine: On the Conditions that Govern the Body's State.
The constitution is affected by what is moderate or extreme — by strengthening or weakening agents, and by what is written concerning the nature of the body. The physician considers these factors: motion and rest, heat and cold, the opposing and the complementary, and the preservation of equilibrium.
As for the body's natural tendency, it seeks balance through the quality of its nourishment. Whatever exceeds this causes deviation. One must consider what restores the body, what purifies it, and when conditions are appropriate for treatment. If the motion is of the productive kind, it will reduce and resolve. If it is of the assimilative kind, it will nourish and build up. As for rest, it produces coldness and the loss of vital spirit and animal faculty.
Chapter Eleven: On the Faculties and Their Classification.
Know that rest and stillness strongly resemble the condition of sleep.

translation:
Right Page (Page 120 right):

But what is specifically notable among the great physicians is that the deficient measure strengthens all the physician's faculties. The merit lies in both aspects — in the inclination and the direction of the appropriate faculties. Many a physician follows the path of sustenance, and whatever nourishment comes to him, he distributes and governs it. The fundamentals are established first. The stimulants of the body must not be neglected, and support must be given to the pillars, so that none are left without foundation. The matter of nobility is maintained as long as the body's strength is upheld — entering into it the essence of what is needed, settling in it what is necessary. The physician must know that the people's strength depends on proper regulation, and that without this, the regulatory faculty cannot connect what is needed for greatness. It is not by the path of mere flow over matter, but by the path of dissolution — for when the dissolving faculty is well connected, it draws from the outermost layers. The great among them are not diminished when the fundamentals of nutrition are followed. Thus the support becomes established for the one receiving treatment, and for all matters of health. If the matter is prolonged and neglected, strangeness appears, and disorder and mixture follow. The lower faculty collects all of this together. If one goes to excess, the brain's temperament is corrupted from its foundation, and the humors become disordered. The extremes of the faculties are diminished, and the vital pneuma produces at that point the conditions described.

Left Page:

The vital faculties and their associated strengths maintain the brain's connections, and whatever is drawn toward the body's composition is prevented from causing excess. The flow of nutrients is prevented from accumulating excessively in the composition, and the matter is kept from being overwhelmed. The balance of forces and their proper distribution restores conditions to their natural state, so that nothing results except sound sleep. The body is neither spread thin by heat nor contracted by cold, and this is evident from the general conditions — none of the categories are left without their due. The corrective faculty applies itself, and one finds in the judgments of physicians its effects everywhere. Every component is held in the compounding vessel, with the breath flowing through what is required. The similar conditions are grouped together, combining similar accidents into one, as happens in the flow of pneuma. Whatever reaches the interior and the exterior — the superfluities are expelled, and what remains settles. What is heard from the flow of substance passes through the innermost channels, and what appears outwardly is governed accordingly. The conditions of both the apparent and the hidden are thereby regulated. Death and dissolution do not occur when the accidents are at their natural level and conditions remain within normal bounds. The internal mover does not dissolve by movement, but rather what is inside remains at a balanced level. It is when sadness, grief, and excessive mental preoccupation occur that what has been described persistently takes hold — this is always a sign and an indication.

I mean the questions concerning the types of treatment with chronic conditions, and in the category of those for whom a single expulsion is not practically possible. There is no need to seek a single expulsion, since if the opposing factor is present in it as an element, then it cannot be surrendered, for the matter has appeared after the resolution and the completion of treatment. The organ cannot be brought to completion unless the humors are first corrected, and the astringent quality of the excretion clarifies the color and refines the perception of the recognizable signs of the condition. What we have mentioned is the basis of its comparable qualities, for they are the foundations of its good nature. If the newborn's account is connected with its proper qualities, and if it is to be balanced, then the subject has been made compliant, and all its states have been heard. The matter of the temperament is such that no substitute treatment is possible unless it is perpetual. This chapter addresses the principles of harm to the human being from every angle and the afflictions in the multiplied organ. One must address the connected treatment of the cause of the formations, and what pertains to it, correcting each thing. Every composition of the human being and what is produced from it, only its nature determines how it shall be. One should speak only of its aspects and what benefits it, describing and attributing to it the proper terms.

Left Page:

Where the patient is treated inwardly according to the physician's approach, except that we have only established its use based on the proportion of what relates to it. The agent with its quality appears and is composed from what it attracts from this goodness, so that it absorbs and settles, and from its being established and its cooling it becomes an attraction. Its composition and its natural characters are such that the human faculty acts as its basis to preserve and protect. From his statement and its depiction and what it contains, it is said: what is needed for the prevention of corruption, and its comparison in terms of its qualities is what has been established for it and belongs to it essentially. The human being is changed by its agent, the generated one, and produced from the heat which is removed from the coldness of what it belongs to. The treatment of the human being, if it is a case of a deficient mixture, is that it should belong to a neighboring organ. The generated one is not formed, and its matter is not established, for the agent is what causes the effect and the outcome of it. The generated one is produced in a natural way and is gathered from other than what is imagined, by substitution. The abstract qualities are composed because the four qualities provide the subtle material aspect as its agent; and when it is absorbed, the organ becomes sound. Together, the analogy of it is that bodies are commanded by what is decreed, and the state is in the storehouse. Its natural quality is composed in the human being and he produces from it what is appropriate to the quality as its nature. What is reached from what is understood, and the result of its type, is the preservation of the balance of the matter according to what is most correct.

translation:
Right page:

Regarding its spreading and originating properties: it is not possible to prepare and compose [a remedy] that acts on simple [substances] in the manner of those simple ones. For those qualities belong only to the primary constituents, which give the compound its temperament. Rather, just as the muscle benefits from the one who strikes it, receiving from the temperament the same faculty that [the striker] possesses — likewise with physicians: every plant and animal [substance] that is beneficial should be used as a substitute for salt. The salt's properties should be understood through its temperament, and the compound should be distinguished [from its parts]. It is not the salt itself that acts, but rather through its coldness, moistness, dryness, or lack thereof, its taste and size indicating the strength of its color and properties. Thus we distinguish from among the grain-based [substances] those with a strong quality, coming after the temperament. The compound acts like water, cooling when its qualities come from a hot [source], and it should be treated as water when these qualities are cold. If it acts in coldness and the action is known to proceed in a descending manner from one level to another, then action descending below will not descend further without basis. Therefore, this knowledge comes from the compound's form and its specific nature. The temperament cannot be characterized by its qualities alone, nor by the qualities of the compound's temperament without considering its full nature. As for nourishment, it cannot be grasped without [understanding] the temperament.

Left page:

Returning to the matter of neutralizing [a substance's] pure quality — what is meant by the excellence of absorbed versus applied [remedies]: We say that when something is ingested or applied externally, [the body's] faculty receives it through its power; this is one of two meanings of "through the faculty." The bodies that receive [the remedy] from the body act through the power, moving through and affecting the body. Thus when the action proceeds to its limit — to the highest degree, directed toward the organ which has primary need — the faculty acts on it in two ways: first, through actual effect; and second, by directing toward it what is carried to the interior, so that [the faculty] accepts it. Thus sulfur [for example] is like the faculty in that it brings [the remedy] toward what is needed. We say secondly that when [a substance] is directed inward and distributed among the elements, it cannot act upon them except through what [the faculty] accomplishes for it, so that the faculty of what is applied [topically] is always aided. Thus [the drug] acts as if through the faculty. This is like the faculty that we mentioned — like the action of harmful things and like the action of poison, which cannot be administered orally. Medicines [therefore] hold the primary position of being administered by ingestion.

translation:
Right page:

The body has many things that are agreeable to it, such as something that may dissolve and cool our companion, or warm it — not merely by its heat being agreeable to it. Even if its nature opposes it in such and such a way, the action is stronger than that. But we do not intend that harm should befall it; rather the natural thing is only partly so. If it opposes everything at the level of harm to it, it should be applied so that it does not harm the substance itself. But we do not intend the indication of the substance except at the fourth level, which is that it should be. That is the property: to possess and describe. This is the specific characteristic of difficult medicaments. This is what occurs through quality. As for possession, it weakens and softens — and these are among its properties.

What enters the body forcibly between them — such as the flowing of the body quickly, as in a purgative, or with many things that pass from the body and dissipate — what resembles the body in its substance resembles it, and what resembles it is the nutriment. What is absolute — that which has no resemblance to it — is the medicament. And what passes over the body and is not fully assimilated: either it has departed from the body in the end, and the physician fails; or it does not depart entirely, and it becomes what ascends to another body or is transformed. The faculty first either becomes related to the body, or is not related to it by way of resemblance — and that is the nutriment.

Left page:

The medicament: if it has no resemblance to it, it is the absolute medicine. The second category is the action of the medicament — that which has no direct relation to our body and is of a particular kind — it is the name "absolute" for us. That which does not depart from the body, remaining within it, acts through the interaction of qualities and spiritual forces. But the faculty of the body acts through the divine power and the interaction of qualities and spiritual forces within it. The physician works upon the body in its natural modes, and the natural force and its vigor are well established. The constitution of the body relies on its nature — the nature of its temperament is sound within it, dissolving the wind. The one who manages it directs and moves it, and its temperament becomes sound in capturing the wind. Its governors control the many forces, the compounds, and others — things established over the duration of the body. The earth with its physicians and the two physicians — when God brings about a transformation, the transformation increases in the two courses. The grief and prevention and relief rest upon the foundations established for the body. These foundations — as if they were arranged upon it — and the body by this medicine, and from its substance and nature by this medicine and the medicine acts upon the body, improving and correcting its quality — thus facilitating the body — and in its quality, what facilitates the body, and what the body acts upon such as garlic and everything — and he does not increase it. So by the modification of its use — when the use is established — it becomes like the sound physicians. And through warmth and dryness, its dissolution increases, but God knows best, and He is the observer.

إنما كل يابس منها بن الكيفية الترابية تي يبدل الأسما له فالجفو كمعني في المزاج لانه من المزاج ثم يبدأ من الله احاد منه ومن اللون يصحن الكلك في المزاج والأدم المذيبه فما قبلها قبل المذاب به ومنها أما قابي ب الغذليبة كان لما عذريه نفسها منها ما أتى قريبه الطبائع الحجم المكر السراب فيح الضرب والقسم منها ما سلامت الجزء الاقيم ومنها ما من اسبدل كا لاغريبه الذنابه وقولان اثنان أسندنا الك البدن بكيفسه وكنيسه ابما بكيسه نهما عرفت ذلك وابما بكيسه فذلك امابات يد وعرور الغنه في البدر الدالمعنه ومن أنضر فوريث القيل ولا إنادة فيهم الذلل سبرده وابما اللهم لما أن عرض منهما عقدة فسقت فأت المعونة كا انها انما اسبحن عرشه كذلك وحسبت عنهما الضلاح لن غريبه ومقول اضا ان اذنا أسنده لطيف من كثيف من ومنبس بذلك والتطف من الاقيم والكثيف ما تولدمنه ودرمن وكل أسملت وتولدمنه ودرفن والكثيف ما تولدمنه درمن وكل التلطيف الاثمار وابما يان يكون كيف امنيده ما ان كان كبير امر الحجر المحتن إذا الكيرت أنده كبيره الكرالكوت والقم فيح الصر المحتن والكيرت أنده كبيره الذا لان كريمه من نحسل الحال لمذنا والكثف المقلب لمذنا الجن

الصفحة اليسرى:

بالعديد وبالإذعان وبايتهمه فا الفتخيل اسعا لهما الله فالطير ومثال الكيت لكيبر الاسنل المذلوف يلم اليمر ومنا الطبيعية فانسل الأدب اما الطلاب بالتوال الموقا والكتبه منه المال المتاح بل الدوران عا سنيبه بابها ثان كل يابس يرمن صل الكيس وردى الكيمن وكبون محي الكيس ومنها ما للطبيعة لكبرا الحرين الحن اليف وهمها اصب الطال المال القلم منا الاقسام في اللطيف القبل لا الحرى والمتلاح والذيات والمباع الاقدي الفذل المذال الطيب المذال الكيس في المجل والجزء ولك الكعول ومثال الكتب اللطبف الكذب الكيس البهيم ولم الهواعض ومثالة اللكت الكيش الحن لهذا الكيس البذ ولم والحجم منزلة اللكتان لكيت إكليهما الذي الذعد اكل المجل خم التواذ لحم لقيط امام الذبن ومثال اللكشنا للكيس ونهذ الطين ولم البط أمام الكريم ومثال اللكت الذبن ومثال اللكشنا للكيسه التيرد ولم البط لطن الادمند

[بخط أحمر:] الفضـل الذا ذريع في الحول

المبا اذا الماكر من الاركان كان من جلد الاركان الله وجعل من منها الاثمار فان جملته أسنا وفي لاثه أسند المعلول ومنصو وانبه وابما طنا إذا الماكن لابست ولانك وابما الوقا من أن يهاب بمثلوا الذي هما المباد ولدية ولانه وعرف ومنها ولك في تلك الاسبد ومن رفع ولك
translation:
Right Page:

Every dry element among them derives from the earthy quality, which gives names to things, and dryness has a meaning in temperament, since it originates from temperament. Then it begins from God as a unity, and from color the components are preserved. In temperament and in the humors what is dissolved: whatever accepts dissolution is accepted, and among them there is that which is absorbent. The nourishing elements: what is close in nature to them partakes of the natural constitution and the volume of the mirage. The part and the category among them: some preserve the integrity of the portion of the upright humor, and some are replaced by the strange and the tails. Two statements: we attribute to the body two qualities, its density and its composition. As for its composition, we have recognized that; and as for its density, that involves certain properties and passages. The faculty in the body and its meaning: whoever distills the fine from the coarse will find that the fine is subtle and the coarse is what is generated from it, and every refinement produces fruits. As for whether it is light or heavy: if the stone aggregates in the retort and becomes large, this is significant. The noble one: from the correction of the state and the disposition, making clear what is subtle and what is thick.

Left Page:

By multiplicity and by acknowledgment and by attribution, God enables the transformation of things, and the example of the large and the small is the natural disposition which guides toward the proper conduct. The attraction toward equilibrium and toward the written record from which wealth and circulation flow — everything dry is connected to the origin of the constitution and the quality of the humors. Among them is that which pertains to the natural faculty for the great arts of harmony. The subtle category precedes the coarse and the compounded. The types and the varieties are the fine, the fluid, the noble, the constitution in the whole and the part. The example of the thick subtle: the obscure constitution in the faculty, and the opposite of it is the constitution of the fine and the deep. The degree of the two: both together in the articulation of the whole and the mass. The light and the delicate: the example of the fine soil and the clay. The great example: the fine soil and its constitution.

[In red ink:] Chapter on the Rapid Transformation of Conditions

As for the elements: when the compound of the elements comes from the body of the elements of God, composed from among them as fruits, their totality is connected in its essence to the cause and its composition. As for when the place is not suitable and is not fixed, and the condition is that it should be feared as equivalent to that which is intended, and recognition of that, and elevation of it.

الصفحة اليمنى:

جزء من لسان والحنك المبسط لا يصعب إلى موضع الدبوبة ملك مواضون الأسنان نعام مركب كالما رهم سبس في قبيل البند إذا مفعه وذلقه ثامذا المالمروف وأمذا إلى لأستصنع عن عنه هفه في فأرارأمذندا والبا بخلف لا في جوهر المابه وبكرع ستطفا الطهما يحب لكيفاء الويعلب عليها ول البابا ماء البنون ولا كأل البيون بكرا البيوت المروءة الأرض ألق لا تنقل سطر شما ستي من البوأل الكيفاء البربة أم لكن جزيبة فكيكون أوثب أن لا سفن عقبه الأضنبه لكرلتي منطبه حتن من البجزيه تبركل عبر تبن بل التي تقع مع ذلك باربه لأكل يأبه بالجاربه المدكيه للمشتر إلى البإيار فأن فاهما ملكتها المجاربه فضبله لما الآلكن فياكاثبت بالكنت ورداه لاكنشها بالأفورد الأسر تاعلم أن البأس المتكون طبقه المبنل شنبر أتي جمعي عليك إلحجاأ ذاب البطيم فوأل المانوأ بذبنه الجزء مأ ثلكبه وروعفه بالحأن لأعفأن ألك لكه عبل أن يكون طبقن بملحلما كأن والستيه المكأن باسنه والأعفر والفه ذلك فأن أشيكن كأن أما الغر المأسدبل الجزئبه وسبل كبريه ماخأ لطه الطبعه ماند إلى الشمس فجموأه نتجرئه إلى الملك رث وبضوصا إلى الصبي مفن هوفضل

الصفحة اليسرى:

لاسماً إذا بذ عبدل عن مبذه وما بوبجته إلى المسالك إلى المجزيه به الجنوب ركذ وخصوصا سهذه والبجنوب باللبريني يعدلين من ماضنه غالبه مع ساير الفضايل والأصل وباكأن يكن هالصنفه كاز عذا نأنصت إله علو ولا بلـ الجرارأتجز بذه من البولبأ لأولبك لأوكان حقبفا كون منع الوزن منع المبرد وبكن بـخلطها لارذا في الاصبف ما لاقي لاشا ما تلك الميه والتجه ولا بكن مع الأمذار من إلى لانيف سبع مترومحا بية وفذه وفطه وماطبور فه ذاعلن أن أوزن بن أزله من الأسون بن المألمه بس في المروعناك الميه المنوله المألمه بـ آكل المول الأفضل وبونبه بربس بزن الكيكات وبونبه بربس ما بن يخلفن وقطبان أن ماشائه أن شاور فأن أوزن مرحفأن أحفيفا المالمر وزيأ للمالمذا الذي خطبه اخذفن ضل والأصبل والمطبر بماصلبه الماءالرذ فأن إكن ذلك والطبق فأن ما إلى المطبوخ علي ما أسهده الأعلا أولي بهما وا سمع الأعداد إلى بذه إلى البقيا المطبوأ بذه من إلى لأن المطبوفن إلى لا ذلك المطبوخ يصد طلبه بذه بسمع لا كيفه ما يطبع في الطيم ارذن لذا ما كنفأ لاكنف البيأن بلم أن البإ أن المما فه حقن إلي بسمه مأسأله الجزيرا في الطاطنه والكثأنه ولا بسط نبر بكر كل لكنن الماء فأما البأسا بذ ادكفهه البرد علها وأما طيه بسدبه مبر من الاجزراء
translation:
Right Page:

A part of the tongue and the flat palate does not easily reach the place of the flow; the positions of the teeth are compound like a remedy for the disease in the region of the gums. When it is chewed, its sharpness, when it is well known, and when it is sought to extract from it, it differs in its essence from what it contains; it draws out the humor of the teeth and does not reach the nature of water. The plants of the earth do not transfer moisture, and they have a quality that is subtle and soft. The nature of such things is that they do not transfer; rather they settle and stay fixed. Each branch of the compound holds together, and for each related element its paired counterpart responds. Know that the physician must understand the layers of the compound element, and what is contained therein in terms of its composition, properties, and qualities. In order for the layers to be in balance, one must consider its moistness and dryness. If it comes to the sun, let it be brought to the ruler and especially to the young, the best of which is more excellent.

Left Page:

When one turns away from the natural passages toward the southern region, and especially near it and the southern channel, it corrects the excess from its properties, and together with all other virtues and the original substance, it ensures that this type is confirmed and elevated. It prevents the weight of the cold from increasing. Mix it in summer with lukewarm water so that its temperament is not disturbed, and combine it with seven measured and weighed portions. Know that the balance of its elements from what is composed in its nature — the best of essentials is to measure the compound and balance it. Whether it is diluted or concentrated, it should be moderate and mild in weight. That which is taken as the base element, together with the boiled and the cooled water — know this: the cooking must be done properly according to the best method. Listen to the quantities up to the remainder — the cooked portion reaches no further than that. Try to understand what is cooked in the broth; note what becomes clear and what becomes thickened, for the nature of the matter is such. As for what settles after it is cooled, and what remains of the parts — these represent the most excellent.
